text: What is a token, and why do LLM APIs bill and limit by tokens rather than words?
ideal_key_points: A token is a subword unit produced by a tokenizer such as BPE, not a whole word | Roughly 3 to 4 English characters or about 0.75 words per token on average | The model processes and predicts tokens, so compute and memory scale with token count | Both input and output tokens count toward context limits and cost, often priced differently

text: What is a context window in a large language model?
ideal_key_points: Maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in one request | Includes system prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents and the generated output | Content beyond the window must be truncated, summarized or retrieved selectively | Larger windows increase cost and latency and do not guarantee the model uses all content well

text: What does the temperature parameter control when generating text from an LLM?
ideal_key_points: Temperature scales the logits before softmax | Low temperature makes the distribution sharper and output more deterministic | High temperature flattens the distribution and increases diversity and randomness | Use low values for extraction or classification and higher values for creative tasks

text: What is hallucination in LLMs?
ideal_key_points: Model generates fluent, confident content that is factually wrong or unsupported | Arises because the model predicts plausible tokens rather than verifying facts | Examples include fake citations, invented APIs or wrong numbers | Especially risky in domains like legal, medical or finance

text: Explain top-p or nucleus sampling and how it differs from top-k sampling.
ideal_key_points: Top-k samples only from the k most likely tokens regardless of their probabilities | Top-p samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p | Top-p adapts the candidate set size to model confidence | Usually tune either temperature or top-p rather than both aggressively

text: Why do LLMs sometimes struggle with tasks like counting letters in a word or reversing strings?
ideal_key_points: Models see subword tokens, not individual characters | A word like strawberry may be one or a few tokens, hiding its letters | Character-level operations require knowledge the model does not directly observe | Mitigations include spelling out characters, using tools or code execution

text: What is the difference between a base model and an instruction-tuned or chat model?
ideal_key_points: Base model is pretrained only on next-token prediction over large text corpora | Instruction-tuned model is further trained with SFT on instruction and response pairs | Chat models are often also aligned with preference tuning like RLHF or DPO | Base models continue text, while chat models follow instructions and use a chat template with roles

text: Explain at a high level what self-attention does in a transformer.
ideal_key_points: Each token is projected into query, key and value vectors | Attention weights come from softmax of scaled query-key dot products | Output for each token is a weighted sum of value vectors, mixing in context from other tokens | Multiple heads learn different relationships, and causal masking prevents attending to future tokens in decoders

text: Why does Hindi or Tamil text often consume more tokens than English for the same content, and what are the practical consequences?
ideal_key_points: Tokenizer vocabularies are trained mostly on English-heavy data, so Indic scripts are split into more pieces | The same sentence can take several times more tokens | Leads to higher cost, higher latency and less usable context window | Mitigations include models with Indic-aware tokenizers, translation pipelines or measuring token counts per language

text: Walk me through how an autoregressive LLM generates a response token by token, including what the KV cache does.
ideal_key_points: Model computes a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token given all previous tokens | A token is chosen by greedy or sampling decoding and appended to the input | Loop repeats until a stop token or max token limit | KV cache stores keys and values of previous tokens so each step only computes attention for the new token | KV cache memory grows with sequence length and batch size

text: What causes hallucinations, and what techniques would you use to reduce them in a production application?
ideal_key_points: Causes include gaps or staleness in training data, pressure to always answer, and decoding randomness | Ground answers with RAG and instruct the model to answer only from provided context | Allow the model to say it does not know and require citations | Lower temperature, add verification steps or self-consistency checks | Measure with faithfulness evals and human review

text: What is the lost in the middle problem with long context windows, and how does it affect how you design prompts?
ideal_key_points: Models tend to use information at the start and end of long contexts better than the middle | Simply stuffing more documents can reduce accuracy | Place the most relevant content near the beginning or end and repeat key instructions | Retrieve and rerank fewer, more relevant chunks instead of maximizing context

text: Compare setting temperature to zero with using a higher temperature. Is temperature zero fully deterministic in practice?
ideal_key_points: Temperature zero approximates greedy decoding by picking the most likely token | Higher temperature increases diversity but also error and format-break risk | Temperature zero is not guaranteed deterministic due to floating point non-associativity, batching and GPU kernel differences | Provider model updates can also change output, so use seeds where supported and design for variance

text: Why is attention cost quadratic in sequence length, and what techniques do modern models use to handle long contexts efficiently?
ideal_key_points: Every token attends to every other token, giving an n by n score matrix | Compute and memory for attention grow as O of n squared | FlashAttention reduces memory traffic by tiling without changing results | Sliding window, sparse attention, grouped-query attention and KV cache compression reduce cost | Position methods like RoPE scaling help extend context length

text: Explain the difference between prefill and decode phases in LLM inference and why they have different performance bottlenecks.
ideal_key_points: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel and builds the KV cache | Prefill is compute-bound and determines time to first token | Decode generates one token at a time and is memory-bandwidth bound | Continuous batching, speculative decoding and KV cache management mainly improve decode throughput | Long prompts raise TTFT while long outputs raise total latency

text: How do mixture-of-experts models work, and what are their trade-offs compared to dense models for serving?
ideal_key_points: MoE layers contain many expert feed-forward networks and a router that selects top-k experts per token | Only a fraction of parameters are active per token, so compute per token is lower than parameter count suggests | All experts must still be held in memory, so memory requirements stay high | Load balancing losses are needed to avoid expert collapse | Serving needs expert parallelism and can suffer from uneven routing and communication overhead

text: What is the difference between zero-shot and few-shot prompting?
ideal_key_points: Zero-shot gives only the instruction with no examples | Few-shot includes a handful of input and output examples in the prompt | Few-shot helps the model learn format, style and edge cases in context | Few-shot costs more tokens and examples can bias outputs

text: What is a system prompt, and how is it different from a user message?
ideal_key_points: System prompt sets the role, rules, tone and constraints for the whole conversation | User messages carry the per-turn request or input | Models are trained to give system instructions higher priority | System prompts are not a security boundary and can be leaked or overridden by injection

text: What is chain-of-thought prompting?
ideal_key_points: Asking the model to reason step by step before giving the final answer | Improves accuracy on multi-step math, logic and reasoning tasks | Can be triggered by instructions or by few-shot examples with worked reasoning | Increases output tokens, so cost and latency go up

text: How do you choose good few-shot examples, and what can go wrong with them?
ideal_key_points: Examples should be representative, diverse and cover edge cases | Format of examples must exactly match the desired output format | Label imbalance or ordering can bias the model toward certain answers | Model may copy surface content from examples | Dynamic selection of similar examples via embeddings can improve results

text: How would you get an LLM to reliably return valid JSON that matches a schema?
ideal_key_points: Use provider structured output or JSON mode with a JSON schema where available | Constrained decoding guarantees syntactically valid output | Validate with a library like Pydantic and retry with the error message on failure | Keep schema simple with clear field descriptions and enums | Low temperature reduces format errors

text: What are the key elements of a well-structured prompt for a production task?
ideal_key_points: Clear role and task description | Relevant context and input clearly delimited, for example with XML tags or headings | Explicit output format and constraints | Examples for tricky cases | Instructions for what to do when information is missing or the request is out of scope

text: What is prompt injection, and how is it different from jailbreaking?
ideal_key_points: Prompt injection is untrusted input containing instructions that override the developer's instructions | Jailbreaking is a user trying to bypass the model's safety training to get disallowed content | Injection targets the application and can cause data exfiltration or unwanted tool actions | Indirect injection comes through retrieved documents, web pages or emails rather than the user directly

text: Your prompt works well in testing but gives inconsistent output formats in production. How would you debug and fix it?
ideal_key_points: Collect and inspect failing production inputs through logs or traces | Look for input differences such as length, language or unusual content that testing missed | Tighten format instructions, add examples, use structured outputs and lower temperature | Add a validation and retry or repair step | Add failing cases to a regression eval set before changing the prompt

text: When does chain-of-thought help, and when can it hurt or be unnecessary, especially with reasoning models?
ideal_key_points: Helps on multi-step reasoning, math and planning tasks | Unnecessary for simple lookup, classification or extraction and adds latency and cost | Reasoning models already think internally, so explicit step-by-step prompts add little and can interfere | Stated reasoning is not always faithful to how the model reached the answer | Separate reasoning from the final answer when parsing output

text: How would you version, test, and roll out changes to prompts in a team setting?
ideal_key_points: Store prompts in version control or a prompt registry, separate from code | Run every change against an eval dataset and compare with the baseline | Pin model versions together with prompt versions | Roll out gradually with A/B tests or canary traffic | Log prompt version with every request for traceability and rollback

text: Compare prompt chaining with a single large prompt for a multi-step task like extracting data from invoices and then validating it.
ideal_key_points: Chaining splits work into focused steps, each easier to prompt, test and debug | Intermediate outputs can be validated in code between steps | Chaining adds latency, cost and error propagation across steps | A single prompt is simpler and faster but harder to debug and less reliable on complex tasks | Deterministic checks like totals matching line items are better done in code than by the LLM

text: How would you defend an LLM application against indirect prompt injection coming from retrieved web pages or emails?
ideal_key_points: No prompt-only defense is complete, so assume injection will sometimes succeed | Clearly delimit untrusted content and instruct the model to treat it as data | Apply least privilege to tools and require human confirmation for sensitive actions | Prevent data exfiltration channels such as auto-rendered links or images with URLs | Use injection classifiers, output filtering and separate privileged and quarantined LLM roles

text: What is retrieval-augmented generation, and what problem does it solve?
ideal_key_points: RAG retrieves relevant documents at query time and adds them to the prompt | Grounds answers in private or up-to-date data the model was not trained on | Reduces hallucination and enables citations | Cheaper and easier to update than retraining or fine-tuning for knowledge

text: What is chunking in a RAG pipeline, and why is it needed?
ideal_key_points: Splitting documents into smaller pieces before embedding and indexing | Embeddings of very long text get diluted and lose specific meaning | Chunks must fit in the embedding model limit and the LLM context | Retrieval returns focused passages instead of whole documents

text: What are the main stages of a basic RAG pipeline from ingestion to answer?
ideal_key_points: Load and parse documents, then clean and chunk them | Embed chunks and store them with metadata in a vector index | At query time embed the question and retrieve top-k similar chunks | Insert retrieved chunks into the prompt and generate an answer, ideally with citations

text: Compare fixed-size chunking, recursive chunking, and semantic chunking.
ideal_key_points: Fixed-size splits by token or character count, simple but can cut sentences and ideas | Recursive splitting tries separators like paragraphs then sentences to respect structure | Semantic chunking splits where embedding similarity between sentences drops | Structure-aware chunking by headings or sections often works best for documents | Choice should be validated with retrieval metrics

text: What is hybrid search, and why combine keyword search like BM25 with dense vector search?
ideal_key_points: Dense search captures semantic meaning and paraphrases | BM25 excels at exact matches like product codes, names and rare terms | Combining them improves recall over either alone | Scores are fused with methods like RRF or weighted normalization

text: What is a reranker, and where does it fit in a RAG pipeline?
ideal_key_points: Reranker reorders an initial candidate set from the retriever | Typically a cross-encoder that scores query and passage together | More accurate than bi-encoder similarity but too slow to run on the whole corpus | Retrieve a larger set like top 50 then rerank to top 5 for the prompt

text: Explain reciprocal rank fusion and why it is used for combining search results.
ideal_key_points: RRF scores each document as the sum of 1 divided by k plus rank across result lists | k is a constant often set around 60 | Uses only ranks, so no need to normalize incompatible scores like BM25 and cosine | Documents ranked well by multiple retrievers rise to the top

text: How do you handle metadata filtering in RAG, for example restricting results to a user's department or a date range?
ideal_key_points: Store metadata such as source, department, date and access level with each chunk | Apply filters in the vector database query rather than after retrieval | Pre-filtering guarantees correctness but can hurt ANN recall if filters are very selective | Post-filtering may return too few results | Access control filters must be enforced server side, never by the LLM

text: Your RAG bot answers confidently from the wrong document. How do you investigate?
ideal_key_points: Trace the request to see the retrieved chunks, their scores and the final prompt | Determine whether retrieval failed or generation ignored the right context | Check chunking, metadata, duplicate or outdated documents and embedding quality for that query | Fix with hybrid search, reranking, metadata filters or better chunking | Add the case to an eval set and measure context precision and faithfulness

text: How do you choose chunk size and overlap, and how would you validate the choice?
ideal_key_points: Chunk size trades recall and specificity against context noise | Small chunks are precise but lose context, large chunks dilute embeddings and waste tokens | Overlap avoids splitting facts across chunk boundaries but increases index size | Choose based on document structure and query type | Validate with recall at k or MRR on a labelled question set

text: What is query rewriting or query expansion in RAG, and when would you use techniques like HyDE?
ideal_key_points: User queries are often short, ambiguous or depend on chat history | Rewriting turns follow-up questions into standalone queries | Multi-query expansion generates variants and merges results to improve recall | HyDE generates a hypothetical answer and embeds it to search, matching document style | Adds latency and an extra LLM call, so use when retrieval recall is the bottleneck

text: How would you make a RAG system cite its sources, and how do you check the citations are real?
ideal_key_points: Give each chunk an ID and source metadata in the prompt | Instruct the model to cite chunk IDs for each claim, or use structured output | Validate that cited IDs exist in the retrieved set | Check citation support with an NLI model or LLM judge that the chunk entails the claim | Show citations as links to the source document for users

text: How would you handle tables, PDFs with complex layouts, and scanned documents in a RAG ingestion pipeline?
ideal_key_points: Use layout-aware parsers rather than naive text extraction | Apply OCR or a vision model for scanned pages | Convert tables to markdown or HTML and keep headers with each row group | Preserve section headings and page numbers as metadata | Spot check parsing quality since bad parsing caps retrieval quality

text: When would you choose a long-context model over RAG, and when is RAG still better?
ideal_key_points: Long context suits small corpora, whole-document reasoning and tasks needing global understanding | RAG scales to large corpora that exceed any context window | RAG is cheaper and faster per query because it sends fewer tokens | Long contexts suffer from lost in the middle and higher latency | Hybrids retrieve whole relevant documents into a long context, and prompt caching can cut costs

text: Design an ingestion pipeline that keeps a RAG index fresh when source documents are updated or deleted frequently.
ideal_key_points: Track document IDs, versions and content hashes to detect changes | Use change events or scheduled incremental syncs instead of full re-indexing | Delete or upsert all chunks belonging to a changed document atomically | Handle deletions and permission changes promptly to avoid leaking stale data | Monitor index lag and keep re-embedding jobs idempotent

text: Design a RAG-based customer support bot over 10,000 product documents for an Indian e-commerce company. Walk me through ingestion, retrieval, generation and evaluation.
ideal_key_points: Parse and chunk documents with metadata like product category, language and last updated date | Hybrid retrieval with BM25 and multilingual embeddings plus reranking | Grounded prompt with citations and fallback to human agent when confidence is low | Handle Hindi and code-mixed queries and conversation history with query rewriting | Evaluate with a labelled question set, faithfulness metrics and production feedback, and monitor cost and latency

text: Design a multi-tenant RAG system where each enterprise customer's documents must stay strictly isolated.
ideal_key_points: Choose isolation level: separate index or namespace per tenant versus shared index with tenant ID filter | Enforce tenant filters in the backend from authenticated identity, never from the prompt | Also handle document-level permissions within a tenant | Isolate caches, logs and any fine-tuned artifacts per tenant | Test for cross-tenant leakage and consider per-tenant encryption, quotas and noisy-neighbour effects

text: Design a RAG system that answers questions across both structured SQL data and unstructured documents, such as sales figures and policy PDFs.
ideal_key_points: Route queries with a classifier or LLM router to SQL, document retrieval or both | Use text-to-SQL with schema descriptions, read-only access and query validation for structured data | Use vector or hybrid retrieval for documents | Combine results in a final generation step with sources for each part | Evaluate SQL correctness by execution accuracy and document answers by faithfulness

text: What is an embedding in the context of NLP?
ideal_key_points: A dense numeric vector representing the meaning of text | Semantically similar texts have nearby vectors | Produced by an embedding model, often a transformer encoder | Used for semantic search, clustering, classification and RAG

text: What is cosine similarity, and why is it commonly used to compare embeddings?
ideal_key_points: Cosine similarity is the dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their norms | Measures the angle between vectors and ignores magnitude | Ranges from minus 1 to 1, with higher meaning more similar | Many embedding models are trained with cosine-based objectives

text: What is a vector database, and why not just use a normal SQL table?
ideal_key_points: Stores embeddings and supports fast nearest neighbour search | Uses ANN indexes like HNSW or IVF to avoid scanning every vector | Supports metadata filtering alongside similarity search | Normal B-tree indexes cannot efficiently answer similarity queries in high dimensions

text: Compare cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance for embedding search. When do they give the same ranking?
ideal_key_points: Cosine ignores magnitude, dot product includes it, Euclidean measures straight-line distance | For L2-normalized vectors all three give the same ranking | Dot product on unnormalized vectors favors longer vectors | Use the metric the embedding model was trained for

text: How would you choose an embedding model for a RAG project, for example for multilingual Indian-language content?
ideal_key_points: Check benchmark results like MTEB but validate on your own queries and documents | Need multilingual support for Indic languages and code-mixed text | Consider dimension size, max input length, latency and cost | Consider hosted API versus self-hosted open model for data privacy | Measure recall at k on a labelled set before committing

text: What is pgvector, and when would you use it instead of a dedicated vector database like Pinecone, Qdrant or Weaviate?
ideal_key_points: pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension adding a vector type and similarity operators | Supports HNSW and IVFFlat indexes | Good when you already use Postgres and want joins, transactions and filters with relational data | Simpler operations with one database for moderate scale | Dedicated vector databases may scale and tune better for very large or high-QPS workloads

text: What is the difference between exact nearest neighbour search and approximate nearest neighbour search?
ideal_key_points: Exact search compares the query with every vector and is guaranteed correct | Exact search cost grows linearly with corpus size | ANN uses index structures to search a subset and returns most of the true neighbours | ANN trades a small loss in recall for large gains in speed | Recall versus latency is tunable through index parameters

text: Explain how an HNSW index works and what its main tuning parameters control.
ideal_key_points: HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph with sparse upper layers and dense bottom layer | Search starts at the top layer and greedily moves closer to the query, descending layers | M controls the number of neighbours per node, affecting recall and memory | ef_construction controls build quality and build time | ef_search controls the query-time candidate list, trading recall for latency

text: Compare HNSW and IVF indexes.
ideal_key_points: IVF clusters vectors with k-means and searches only the nearest nlist clusters controlled by nprobe | HNSW uses a navigable graph and generally gives better recall and latency | HNSW uses more memory and is slower to build | IVF is more memory efficient and pairs well with product quantization for huge datasets | IVF needs training on representative data and may need retraining as data shifts

text: What is the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder?
ideal_key_points: Bi-encoder embeds query and document separately into vectors | Bi-encoder document embeddings can be precomputed, making search fast at scale | Cross-encoder processes query and document together and outputs a relevance score | Cross-encoder is more accurate but must run per pair, so it is used for reranking a small candidate set

text: You switch to a new embedding model. What do you need to do with your existing index and why?
ideal_key_points: Embeddings from different models live in different incompatible vector spaces | All documents must be re-embedded and the index rebuilt, possibly with a new dimension | Query embeddings must use the same model as the documents | Run old and new indexes in parallel and switch over after evaluating retrieval quality | Store model name and version with vectors to avoid mixing

text: Design a vector search system for 100 million embeddings with low latency and a limited memory budget.
ideal_key_points: Estimate memory, for example 100 million times 768 dimensions times 4 bytes is about 300 GB in float32 | Use compression like product quantization, scalar quantization or binary embeddings with rescoring | Consider IVF-PQ or disk-based indexes like DiskANN | Shard across nodes and replicate for throughput | Measure recall at k against exact search and tune for latency targets

text: What is an AI agent, and how is it different from a single LLM call?
ideal_key_points: An agent uses an LLM in a loop to decide actions toward a goal | It can call tools, observe results and decide next steps | A single call maps input to output with no actions or iteration | Agents add flexibility but also cost, latency and unpredictability

text: What is function calling or tool calling in LLMs?
ideal_key_points: Developer provides tool names, descriptions and parameter schemas to the model | Model outputs a structured request to call a tool with arguments instead of plain text | Application executes the function and returns the result to the model | Lets LLMs fetch live data and take actions

text: What is the ReAct pattern?
ideal_key_points: ReAct stands for reasoning and acting interleaved | Model alternates thought, action and observation steps | Observations from tools feed back into the next reasoning step | Loop ends when the model produces a final answer

text: How does an LLM actually decide to call a tool, and who executes the tool?
ideal_key_points: Tool schemas are included in the prompt and the model is trained to emit tool call outputs | The model chooses a tool based on descriptions and the conversation | The model never executes code itself, the application runtime does | Results are sent back as a tool result message for the next model turn | Application must validate arguments before executing

text: What makes a good tool definition or schema for an LLM agent?
ideal_key_points: Clear, distinct name and description stating when to use and not use the tool | Typed parameters with descriptions, enums and required fields | Small number of non-overlapping tools | Concise, informative return values and helpful error messages the model can act on | Idempotent and safe operations where possible

text: What kinds of memory can an agent have, and how would you implement short-term and long-term memory?
ideal_key_points: Short-term memory is the conversation and scratchpad within the context window | Long context is managed by trimming or summarizing older turns | Long-term memory stores facts or past interactions in a database or vector store | Relevant memories are retrieved and injected into the prompt when needed | Need policies for what to store, updating stale facts and user privacy

text: What is MCP, the Model Context Protocol, and what problem does it solve?
ideal_key_points: MCP is an open protocol for connecting LLM applications to tools and data sources | Servers expose tools, resources and prompts, and clients in host apps connect to them | Standardizes integrations so one server works across many hosts instead of custom glue code per app | Security concerns include trusting third-party servers and tool-based prompt injection

text: Your agent gets stuck in a loop calling the same tool repeatedly. How would you debug and prevent this?
ideal_key_points: Inspect traces of tool calls, arguments and results to find the cause | Common causes are unhelpful errors, ambiguous tool output or unclear stop condition | Return clear error messages and improve tool descriptions | Add max iteration limits, duplicate call detection and budget caps | Add these trajectories to evaluation cases

text: Explain how a state-graph framework like LangGraph models an agent workflow, and why that is useful compared to a free-form loop.
ideal_key_points: Workflow is defined as nodes that update a shared typed state and edges between them | Conditional edges route based on state such as whether a tool call was made | Supports cycles for agent loops with explicit control flow | Checkpointing enables persistence, resuming and human-in-the-loop interrupts | Easier to debug, test and constrain than a fully free-form agent

text: When would you use a deterministic workflow instead of an autonomous agent?
ideal_key_points: Use workflows when steps are known in advance and predictable | Workflows are cheaper, faster, easier to test and more reliable | Agents suit open-ended tasks where the path cannot be predefined | Many production systems combine fixed workflows with limited LLM decision points | Start simple and add autonomy only when it measurably helps

text: How would you add human-in-the-loop approval to an agent that can take actions like sending emails or making refunds?
ideal_key_points: Classify tools by risk, with read-only tools auto-approved and write actions gated | Pause execution and persist state before sensitive actions | Show the human the exact proposed action and arguments to approve, edit or reject | Resume from checkpoint after decision and log everything for audit | Enforce limits like refund caps in code, not just in the prompt

text: Compare a supervisor-style multi-agent architecture with a single agent that has many tools.
ideal_key_points: Single agent is simpler with less latency, but tool selection degrades as tool count grows | Supervisor routes subtasks to specialized agents with focused prompts and tool sets | Multi-agent adds coordination overhead, more tokens and harder debugging | Context passing between agents can lose information | Choose multi-agent only when tasks are separable and specialization measurably improves quality

text: How do you evaluate an agent, given that it takes multi-step trajectories rather than producing a single output?
ideal_key_points: Evaluate final outcome or task success against expected results or end state | Evaluate trajectory, such as correct tool choices, arguments and step count | Track cost, latency and number of LLM calls per task | Use sandboxed environments with mocked or replayable tools for repeatable tests | Run multiple trials due to non-determinism and report success rate

text: Design a multi-agent system that researches a company and writes an investment brief, including orchestration, tool access, and failure handling.
ideal_key_points: Planner or supervisor decomposes the task into research areas like financials, news and competitors | Worker agents use tools such as web search, filings retrieval and a calculator, running in parallel where possible | Writer agent synthesizes findings with citations, and a critic or verifier checks claims | Handle failures with retries, timeouts, budgets and partial results | Persist state, trace every step and evaluate briefs for accuracy and coverage

text: Design an agent that can safely execute SQL queries against a production database to answer business questions.
ideal_key_points: Use a read-only database user or read replica with least privilege | Provide schema descriptions and sample queries for accurate text-to-SQL | Validate generated SQL, block DDL and DML, enforce row limits and timeouts | Enforce row-level and column-level security for sensitive data like PII | Let the agent retry on errors, show the SQL to users and evaluate with execution accuracy

text: Why is evaluating LLM outputs harder than evaluating a traditional classifier?
ideal_key_points: Outputs are open-ended text with many valid answers | No single ground truth label for exact match accuracy | Quality has multiple dimensions like correctness, relevance, tone and safety | Outputs are non-deterministic and sensitive to prompt changes

text: What is a golden dataset or eval set, and why do you need one?
ideal_key_points: A curated set of inputs with expected outputs or grading criteria | Covers common cases, edge cases and known past failures | Lets you compare prompts, models and pipeline changes objectively | Must be versioned and kept separate from examples used in prompts or training | Grows over time from production failures

text: What is LLM-as-a-judge?
ideal_key_points: Using an LLM to grade outputs of another LLM against criteria or a rubric | Can score pointwise or compare outputs pairwise | Scales cheaper and faster than human evaluation | Needs calibration against human labels because judges have biases

text: What are faithfulness and answer relevancy in RAG evaluation?
ideal_key_points: Faithfulness measures whether claims in the answer are supported by the retrieved context | Typically computed by extracting claims and checking each against context | Answer relevancy measures whether the answer addresses the question asked | An answer can be faithful but irrelevant, or relevant but hallucinated

text: What are context precision and context recall, and what do they tell you about a RAG pipeline?
ideal_key_points: Context precision measures how much of the retrieved context is relevant and whether relevant chunks rank high | Context recall measures whether the retrieved context contains all information needed for the reference answer | Low recall points to retrieval misses such as chunking or embedding issues | Low precision means noisy context, which suggests reranking or fewer chunks | They isolate retriever quality from generator quality

text: Compare reference-based metrics like BLEU and ROUGE with LLM-based evaluation for generative tasks.
ideal_key_points: BLEU and ROUGE measure n-gram overlap with reference texts | They are cheap and deterministic but penalize valid paraphrases and miss factual errors | LLM-based evaluation can judge meaning, correctness and style | LLM evaluation costs more, is non-deterministic and has biases | Embedding similarity like BERTScore sits in between

text: What retrieval metrics would you use to evaluate the retriever on its own, like recall at k and MRR?
ideal_key_points: Recall at k is the fraction of queries where a relevant chunk appears in the top k | Precision at k is the fraction of top-k results that are relevant | MRR averages 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant result | NDCG accounts for graded relevance and position | Requires a labelled set of queries with relevant chunk IDs

text: What biases does an LLM judge have, and how do you mitigate them?
ideal_key_points: Position bias favors the first or second option in pairwise comparison | Verbosity bias favors longer answers | Self-preference bias favors outputs from the same model family | Mitigate by swapping order and averaging, using clear rubrics with specific criteria, and using a different model as judge | Calibrate against human labels and use low temperature

text: How would you validate that your LLM judge actually agrees with human judgments?
ideal_key_points: Have humans label a representative sample using the same rubric | Measure agreement with metrics like Cohen's kappa, correlation or accuracy | Analyze disagreement cases and refine the rubric or judge prompt | Compare to inter-human agreement as a ceiling | Re-validate when the judge model or rubric changes

text: Compare pairwise comparison with pointwise scoring for LLM evaluation.
ideal_key_points: Pointwise scores each output independently on a scale or rubric | Pairwise asks which of two outputs is better | Pairwise is more reliable for subtle differences and comparing versions | Pointwise gives absolute scores useful for monitoring and thresholds | Pairwise suffers position bias and scales quadratically with many candidates

text: You changed the prompt and your offline eval score went up, but users complain more. What could explain this?
ideal_key_points: Eval set may not represent real production traffic or new user behaviour | Metric or judge may reward the wrong thing, such as longer answers | Possible overfitting of the prompt to the eval set | Latency, tone or format changes may hurt user experience without hurting scores | Sample and label production conversations and add complaint cases to the eval set

text: How would you build regression tests for an LLM feature in a CI pipeline?
ideal_key_points: Maintain a versioned eval dataset with expected outputs or rubrics | Combine deterministic checks like schema validation and keyword assertions with LLM-judge scores | Set thresholds and compare against baseline rather than requiring exact matches | Run multiple samples or use low temperature to handle non-determinism | Control cost by running a small suite per PR and a full suite nightly

text: How do you evaluate a chatbot in production when you do not have ground truth answers?
ideal_key_points: Collect implicit signals like thumbs up or down, retries, escalations and conversation abandonment | Run reference-free LLM-judge checks for faithfulness, relevance and policy compliance on sampled traffic | Human review of a sampled subset, prioritising low-score or flagged conversations | Monitor drift in topics, latency and cost | A/B test changes on business metrics

text: Design an evaluation pipeline for a RAG application, from dataset creation to offline metrics to online monitoring.
ideal_key_points: Build a dataset from real queries, synthetic questions generated from documents and expert-written cases, reviewed by humans | Measure retrieval separately with recall at k and context precision and recall | Measure generation with faithfulness, answer correctness and citation accuracy using calibrated judges | Run in CI on every prompt, model or index change with baseline comparison | Online sampling with judges, user feedback and dashboards feeding new failures back into the dataset

text: What is fine-tuning an LLM?
ideal_key_points: Continuing training of a pretrained model on a task- or domain-specific dataset | Adapts behaviour, format, style or domain performance | Full fine-tuning updates all weights, while PEFT updates a small subset | Requires curated data, compute and evaluation

text: What is LoRA?
ideal_key_points: Low-Rank Adaptation, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method | Freezes base weights and learns two small low-rank matrices added to weight updates | Trains far fewer parameters, reducing memory and compute | Adapters are small files that can be swapped or merged into the base model

text: What is quantization of a model?
ideal_key_points: Representing weights and sometimes activations with fewer bits, such as INT8 or INT4 instead of FP16 | Reduces memory footprint and can speed up inference | May cause some loss in accuracy | Enables running larger models on smaller GPUs or CPUs

text: How do you decide between prompt engineering, RAG, and fine-tuning for a given problem?
ideal_key_points: Start with prompt engineering because it is cheapest and fastest to iterate | Use RAG when the model needs external, private or frequently changing knowledge | Use fine-tuning to change behaviour, format, style or to specialize a smaller cheaper model | Fine-tuning is poor for injecting frequently updated facts | They can be combined, and the decision should be driven by evals

text: What is QLoRA, and how does it differ from LoRA?
ideal_key_points: QLoRA loads the frozen base model in 4-bit quantization, typically NF4 | LoRA adapters are trained in higher precision on top of the quantized model | Uses tricks like double quantization and paged optimizers to save memory | Allows fine-tuning large models on a single consumer or mid-range GPU | Slightly slower training than LoRA with similar quality

text: What is knowledge distillation, and why would a company distill a large model into a smaller one?
ideal_key_points: A smaller student model is trained to mimic a larger teacher model | Teacher outputs or soft probabilities serve as training targets | Student is cheaper, faster and easier to deploy | Commonly done by generating synthetic data from a large LLM and fine-tuning a small model | Check model provider licence terms on using outputs for training

text: What does a good fine-tuning dataset look like for instruction tuning, and how much data do you typically need?
ideal_key_points: Quality and diversity matter more than raw quantity | Examples should match the exact prompt format and chat template used at inference | Cover edge cases, include refusals or out-of-scope cases where needed | Hundreds to a few thousand high-quality examples often suffice for style or format tasks | Deduplicate, hold out a test set and remove PII

text: Explain the LoRA rank and alpha hyperparameters and which layers you typically apply LoRA to.
ideal_key_points: Rank r sets the inner dimension of the low-rank matrices and thus capacity | Common ranks range from 8 to 64, and higher rank means more parameters and memory | Alpha scales the update, with effective scale alpha divided by r | Typically applied to attention projections such as q and v, often all linear layers including MLP for better quality | Tune learning rate alongside rank

text: Compare supervised fine-tuning with preference tuning methods like RLHF and DPO.
ideal_key_points: SFT trains on demonstration pairs of prompt and ideal response | Preference tuning uses comparisons of chosen versus rejected responses | RLHF trains a reward model then optimizes the policy with RL such as PPO, which is complex and unstable | DPO optimizes directly on preference pairs without a separate reward model or RL loop | Typically SFT comes first, then preference tuning for alignment and quality

text: Your fine-tuned model performs well on your task but has become worse at general instructions. What happened, and how do you fix it?
ideal_key_points: This is catastrophic forgetting, where narrow training overwrites general capabilities | Too many epochs or too high a learning rate makes it worse | Mix in general instruction data with task data | Use PEFT like LoRA, lower learning rate and fewer epochs | Evaluate on both task-specific and general benchmarks before release

text: Compare quantization formats such as INT8, INT4 with GPTQ or AWQ, and GGUF in terms of quality, speed, and deployment target.
ideal_key_points: INT8 usually has minimal quality loss and roughly halves memory versus FP16 | INT4 methods like GPTQ and AWQ use calibration data to minimize error and quarter memory with small quality loss | AWQ protects salient weights based on activation statistics | GGUF is the llama.cpp format targeting CPU and Apple Silicon with mixed quantization levels | Always evaluate the quantized model on your own tasks

text: You have 5,000 labelled support tickets and a budget for one A100 GPU. Plan how you would fine-tune and deploy an open-weights model to classify and draft replies, and how you would know it beats a prompted API model.
ideal_key_points: Clean, deduplicate and redact PII, then split into train, validation and test sets | Use LoRA or QLoRA on a 7B to 8B class open model formatted with its chat template | Evaluate classification with accuracy and F1 and replies with rubric-based judges and human review | Compare against a prompted API baseline on the same test set for quality, latency and cost | Serve with an efficient engine like vLLM with quantization and monitor for drift

text: What are guardrails in an LLM application?
ideal_key_points: Checks and controls applied around the LLM to keep it safe and on-policy | Input guardrails detect injection, toxic content, PII or off-topic requests | Output guardrails check toxicity, PII leaks, hallucination and format | Implemented with rules, classifiers or LLM-based checks

text: What is streaming in LLM APIs, and why does it improve user experience?
ideal_key_points: Tokens are sent to the client as they are generated, often via server-sent events | Users see output after time to first token instead of waiting for the full response | Total generation time is unchanged but perceived latency drops | Makes output validation and moderation harder because content arrives incrementally

text: How would you detect and handle PII in prompts and responses in an LLM application?
ideal_key_points: Detect PII with regex for structured data like Aadhaar, PAN and phone numbers plus NER models | Redact or mask PII before sending to third-party APIs and re-insert if needed | Avoid storing raw PII in logs and traces | Check outputs for leaked PII | Follow data protection law such as India's DPDP Act and provider data retention terms

text: What is prompt caching, and how is it different from semantic caching of responses?
ideal_key_points: Prompt caching reuses the computed KV cache for a repeated prompt prefix on the provider side | Reduces cost and latency for long stable prefixes like system prompts or documents | Requires stable content at the start of the prompt | Semantic caching returns a stored response when a new query is similar enough to a previous one | Semantic caching risks returning wrong answers if the similarity threshold is too loose

text: What is model routing, and how can it reduce cost?
ideal_key_points: Routing sends each request to the most appropriate model | Simple requests go to small cheap models and hard ones to large models | Routing can use rules, a classifier or a cascade that escalates on low confidence | Needs evals to ensure quality does not drop on routed traffic

text: What should you log and trace in an LLM application for observability?
ideal_key_points: Full prompt, response, model name and version and parameters | Token counts, cost, latency including time to first token, and errors | Spans for each step such as retrieval, tool calls and LLM calls in a trace | User feedback and eval scores linked to traces | Redact PII and control access to logs

text: Your LLM feature's monthly API bill has tripled. How would you investigate and reduce costs?
ideal_key_points: Break down cost by feature, user, model and input versus output tokens | Look for causes like growing chat history, retry loops, agent loops or abuse | Trim context, summarize history and reduce retrieved chunks | Use prompt caching, response caching and route to cheaper models | Set per-user rate limits, max tokens and budget alerts

text: How do you handle rate limits, timeouts, and provider outages when calling LLM APIs?
ideal_key_points: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter on 429 and 5xx errors | Set timeouts and respect retry-after headers | Fall back to an alternate model or provider with a compatible prompt | Use queues and request prioritization to smooth traffic | Circuit breakers and graceful degradation messages for users

text: How would you reduce end-to-end latency of an LLM-powered chat feature?
ideal_key_points: Measure time to first token and total latency per step with tracing | Stream responses to users | Use smaller or faster models and reduce output length | Shorten prompts, use prompt caching and parallelize independent calls like retrieval and tool calls | Cache frequent answers and colocate services near the model endpoint

text: Design an LLM gateway that sits in front of multiple model providers with fallbacks, cost limits per team, and logging.
ideal_key_points: Unified API that abstracts provider differences and handles authentication with per-team keys | Routing and fallback chains on errors, timeouts or rate limits | Token counting and cost tracking with per-team budgets, quotas and rate limits | Centralized logging and tracing with PII redaction | Caching, health checks and ability to switch models without client changes

text: Design the guardrails layer for a customer-facing banking chatbot in India, covering input, output, and compliance requirements.
ideal_key_points: Input checks for prompt injection, abuse, off-topic queries and PII masking such as account numbers and Aadhaar | Strict grounding in approved bank content and no financial advice beyond policy | Output checks for hallucinated figures, PII leakage, toxic content and required disclaimers | Sensitive actions require authentication and are executed by backend systems, not the LLM | Audit logs, data residency, RBI and DPDP compliance, human escalation and red-team testing

text: What is speech-to-text, and what is Whisper?
ideal_key_points: Speech-to-text or ASR converts spoken audio into text | Whisper is an open-source ASR model from OpenAI trained on large multilingual weakly supervised data | Uses an encoder-decoder transformer on log-mel spectrograms | Supports transcription in many languages and translation to English

text: What is voice activity detection, and why is it needed in a voice assistant?
ideal_key_points: VAD detects whether an audio segment contains human speech or silence and noise | Used to detect when a user starts and stops speaking, to know when to respond | Avoids sending silence to ASR, saving cost and reducing hallucinated transcripts | Silero VAD and WebRTC VAD are common examples

text: What is a vision-language model?
ideal_key_points: A model that takes images and text as input and generates text | Can describe images, answer questions about them and read text in images | Typically combines a vision encoder with a language model | Used for document understanding, chart reading and visual QA

text: What is the difference between a cascaded voice pipeline and a native speech-to-speech model?
ideal_key_points: Cascaded pipeline chains STT, then LLM, then TTS | Cascaded is modular, easy to debug and lets you pick best components | Cascades add latency at each stage and lose tone and emotion in transcription | Native speech-to-speech models process audio directly with lower latency and preserved prosody | Native models are less controllable and harder to evaluate

text: What factors affect speech recognition accuracy for Indian English and code-mixed speech like Hinglish, and how would you improve it?
ideal_key_points: Accents, code-switching, background noise and domain vocabulary all increase errors | Mixed scripts make output inconsistent, for example Hindi in Devanagari or Roman script | Use models trained on Indian languages or fine-tune on local data | Use prompts or custom vocabulary for domain terms and names | Measure WER on representative Indian test audio

text: What is word error rate, and how is it computed?
ideal_key_points: WER is the standard metric for speech recognition accuracy | Computed as substitutions plus deletions plus insertions divided by number of words in the reference | Uses edit distance alignment between hypothesis and reference | Text should be normalized for case and punctuation first | Can exceed 100 percent and does not weigh important words more

text: How would you extract structured data from scanned invoices using a multimodal LLM versus a traditional OCR pipeline?
ideal_key_points: Traditional pipeline uses OCR, then layout analysis and rules or NER to extract fields | Multimodal LLM reads the image directly and outputs structured JSON for a schema | LLMs handle varied layouts better but can hallucinate values and cost more | Validate with checks like totals matching line items and GSTIN format | Route low-confidence extractions to human review

text: How do you handle barge-in, where a user interrupts a voice bot while it is speaking?
ideal_key_points: Keep VAD running on the microphone while TTS is playing | Use echo cancellation so the bot does not detect its own voice | On detected user speech, stop TTS playback and cancel pending generation | Update conversation history to reflect only what was actually spoken | Tune thresholds to avoid false interruptions from short backchannels like okay

text: How does an image get turned into tokens that a vision-language model can process?
ideal_key_points: Image is split into fixed-size patches, for example 14 by 14 pixels | A vision encoder such as a ViT produces an embedding per patch | A projection layer or adapter maps vision embeddings into the LLM embedding space | Image tokens are interleaved with text tokens in the sequence | Higher resolution means more tokens, so cost scales with image size, and tiling handles large images

text: Design a real-time voice mock-interview bot with under one second of response latency.
ideal_key_points: Stream audio over WebRTC or WebSockets with VAD-based end-of-turn detection | Use streaming STT, then a fast LLM with streaming output | Start TTS on the first sentence chunk rather than waiting for the full reply | Budget latency per stage and measure time from end of speech to first audio | Support barge-in, handle network jitter and evaluate both transcription accuracy and interview quality

text: What is the difference between supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning?
ideal_key_points: Supervised learning trains on labeled input-output pairs, e.g. classification and regression | Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data, e.g. clustering and dimensionality reduction | Reinforcement learning has an agent learn a policy by taking actions and receiving rewards from an environment | Gives a concrete example of each

text: What is overfitting and what is underfitting?
ideal_key_points: Overfitting means the model memorizes training data including noise and generalizes poorly, low train error but high validation error | Underfitting means the model is too simple to capture the pattern, high error on both train and validation | Overfitting relates to high variance and underfitting to high bias | Fixes for overfitting include more data, regularization and simpler models, fixes for underfitting include more capacity and better features

text: What is the difference between a model parameter and a hyperparameter?
ideal_key_points: Parameters are learned from data during training, e.g. weights and biases | Hyperparameters are set before training and control the learning process, e.g. learning rate, tree depth, k in kNN | Hyperparameters are tuned using a validation set or cross-validation, not the training loss | Parameters are what the saved model contains

text: What is gradient descent, in simple terms?
ideal_key_points: An iterative optimization method to minimize a loss function | Computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters | Updates parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient, scaled by the learning rate | Repeats until convergence or a stopping criterion

text: Why do we split data into training, validation and test sets?
ideal_key_points: Training set is used to fit model parameters | Validation set is used for hyperparameter tuning and model selection | Test set is held out and used once for an unbiased estimate of generalization | Reusing the test set for tuning leads to optimistic estimates

text: Explain the bias-variance trade-off.
ideal_key_points: Bias is error from overly simple assumptions, causing underfitting | Variance is error from sensitivity to the specific training set, causing overfitting | Expected error decomposes into bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise | Increasing model complexity typically lowers bias but raises variance, so we seek a balance | Regularization, more data and ensembling are levers to manage it

text: What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularization, and what effect does each have on the weights?
ideal_key_points: L1 adds the sum of absolute weights to the loss, L2 adds the sum of squared weights | L1 drives many weights exactly to zero, giving sparse models and implicit feature selection | L2 shrinks weights smoothly toward zero but rarely to exactly zero | L1 is Lasso and L2 is Ridge in linear regression, Elastic Net combines both | Regularization strength is controlled by a hyperparameter such as lambda or alpha

text: Compare batch gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent and mini-batch gradient descent.
ideal_key_points: Batch uses the whole dataset per update, giving stable but slow and memory-heavy steps | SGD uses one sample per update, fast but noisy | Mini-batch uses a small batch such as 32 to 512 samples, balancing noise and efficiency | Mini-batch exploits vectorization on GPUs and is the default in deep learning | Noise in SGD can help escape sharp minima and saddle points

text: How does the learning rate affect training, and what happens if it is too high or too low?
ideal_key_points: Learning rate scales the size of each parameter update | Too high causes oscillation, divergence or loss going to NaN | Too low causes very slow convergence or getting stuck in poor regions | Can be found with a learning rate range test or tuning on validation | Schedules and adaptive optimizers adjust the effective step size over time

text: What is early stopping and why does it act as a regularizer?
ideal_key_points: Monitor validation loss or metric during training | Stop when it stops improving for a set number of epochs, called patience | Restore the best checkpoint rather than the last one | It limits how far weights move from initialization, reducing effective capacity and overfitting

text: Why is mean squared error typically used for regression and cross-entropy for classification?
ideal_key_points: MSE corresponds to maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise for continuous targets | Cross-entropy corresponds to maximum likelihood for categorical or Bernoulli outputs | Cross-entropy with sigmoid or softmax gives strong gradients when predictions are confidently wrong | MSE with sigmoid outputs leads to small gradients when saturated and slow learning

text: How does momentum improve on plain stochastic gradient descent?
ideal_key_points: Keeps an exponentially weighted moving average of past gradients as a velocity term | Updates use the velocity, typically with a coefficient around 0.9 | Dampens oscillations in high-curvature directions and accelerates along consistent directions | Helps move through ravines, plateaus and small local minima faster | Nesterov momentum computes the gradient at the look-ahead position for better correction

text: Walk me through how the Adam optimizer works.
ideal_key_points: Maintains a first moment estimate, a moving average of gradients, like momentum | Maintains a second moment estimate, a moving average of squared gradients, like RMSProp | Applies bias correction because both moments start at zero | Update divides the first moment by the square root of the second moment plus epsilon, giving per-parameter adaptive learning rates | Common defaults are beta1 0.9, beta2 0.999 and learning rate 1e-3

text: What learning rate schedules have you used, and why would you use warmup?
ideal_key_points: Names schedules such as step decay, exponential decay, cosine annealing, reduce on plateau or one-cycle | Decaying the learning rate lets the model settle into a minimum after fast early progress | Warmup linearly increases the learning rate from a small value over the first steps | Warmup stabilizes early training when Adam moment estimates and normalization statistics are unreliable, especially for transformers and large batch sizes

text: Your training loss keeps decreasing but validation loss starts rising after a few epochs. How would you diagnose and fix this?
ideal_key_points: Identifies this as overfitting | Checks for data issues like train and validation distribution mismatch or leakage | Applies regularization such as dropout, weight decay or data augmentation | Uses early stopping with the best checkpoint | Considers more data, a smaller model or a lower learning rate

text: When would you prefer Huber loss over mean squared error?
ideal_key_points: Huber loss is quadratic for small errors and linear for large errors beyond a threshold delta | It is less sensitive to outliers than MSE because large errors are not squared | It remains differentiable at zero, unlike MAE | Use it when the target has outliers or heavy-tailed noise but you still want smooth optimization

text: Why does L1 regularization produce sparse solutions while L2 does not?
ideal_key_points: The L1 penalty has a constant gradient magnitude regardless of weight size, so it keeps pushing small weights all the way to zero | The L2 penalty gradient is proportional to the weight, so the push vanishes as the weight approaches zero | Geometrically the L1 constraint region is a diamond with corners on the axes, where the loss contours tend to touch it | Proximal methods for L1 use soft-thresholding, which sets small weights exactly to zero

text: What is the difference between Adam and AdamW, and why does it matter?
ideal_key_points: In Adam, L2 regularization is added to the gradient and then rescaled by the adaptive denominator | That means weights with large gradient history get less regularization than intended | AdamW decouples weight decay, applying it directly to the weights separately from the gradient update | Decoupled weight decay generalizes better and is the standard for training transformers

text: Your model's training loss is stuck and barely decreasing from the first epoch. What would you check?
ideal_key_points: Sanity check by overfitting a tiny batch, if it cannot the bug is in the model or pipeline | Verify labels align with inputs and the data loader is not shuffling inputs and labels separately | Check the learning rate, both too high and too low, and the optimizer setup | Check loss function matches the output, e.g. not applying softmax twice before cross-entropy | Inspect gradients for zero or vanishing values, dead ReLUs, bad initialization or unscaled inputs

text: Explain the double descent phenomenon and how it challenges the classical bias-variance picture.
ideal_key_points: Classical view says test error is U-shaped as model complexity grows | Double descent shows test error peaks near the interpolation threshold, where parameters roughly equal the number of samples | Beyond that threshold, test error decreases again as models become heavily overparameterized | Explanation involves implicit regularization of optimizers like SGD choosing minimum norm or smooth interpolating solutions | It also appears versus training epochs and dataset size, and is sensitive to label noise

text: How does k-nearest neighbors make a prediction?
ideal_key_points: Stores the training data, there is no explicit training phase | For a new point, computes distances such as Euclidean to all training points | Takes the k closest points and uses majority vote for classification or average for regression | k is a hyperparameter, small k overfits and large k underfits

text: What is the difference between linear regression and logistic regression?
ideal_key_points: Linear regression predicts a continuous value | Logistic regression predicts a probability for classification by passing a linear combination through the sigmoid function | Linear regression is typically fit with mean squared error, logistic with log loss or cross-entropy | Logistic regression is a linear classifier, its decision boundary is linear in the features

text: What does k-means clustering do?
ideal_key_points: Unsupervised algorithm that partitions data into k clusters | Initializes k centroids, assigns each point to the nearest centroid, then recomputes centroids as cluster means | Repeats until assignments stop changing | Minimizes within-cluster sum of squared distances | k must be chosen in advance

text: How does a decision tree decide where to split?
ideal_key_points: Evaluates candidate features and thresholds at each node | For classification uses impurity measures such as Gini impurity or entropy and information gain | For regression uses reduction in variance or MSE | Chooses the split that maximizes impurity reduction greedily | Stops based on max depth, min samples per leaf or no further gain

text: What is a random forest and why does it usually beat a single decision tree?
ideal_key_points: Ensemble of decision trees trained on bootstrap samples of the data, which is bagging | Each split considers only a random subset of features, decorrelating the trees | Predictions are averaged or majority-voted | Averaging many decorrelated high-variance trees reduces variance without much increase in bias | Provides out-of-bag error estimates and feature importances

text: What is the naive assumption in naive Bayes, and why does it still work well for text classification?
ideal_key_points: Assumes features are conditionally independent given the class | Uses Bayes theorem, posterior proportional to prior times product of feature likelihoods | Assumption is usually false but the class ranking can still be correct even if probabilities are poorly calibrated | Works well for text with bag-of-words because it is fast, needs little data and handles high dimensions | Uses Laplace smoothing to avoid zero probabilities for unseen words

text: How do you choose the number of clusters in k-means?
ideal_key_points: Elbow method plotting within-cluster sum of squares against k and looking for the bend | Silhouette score measuring cohesion versus separation, higher is better | Other criteria such as gap statistic or Davies-Bouldin index | Domain knowledge and business usefulness of the clusters

text: What is PCA and when would you use it?
ideal_key_points: Principal Component Analysis is a linear dimensionality reduction technique | Finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance, the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix or via SVD | Data should be standardized first since PCA is scale sensitive | Choose components by explained variance ratio, e.g. retaining 95 percent | Used for visualization, noise reduction, speeding up models and handling multicollinearity, at the cost of interpretability

text: Compare bagging and boosting.
ideal_key_points: Bagging trains models independently in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages them | Boosting trains models sequentially, each one focusing on the errors of the previous ones | Bagging mainly reduces variance, boosting mainly reduces bias | Random forest is an example of bagging, AdaBoost and gradient boosting are examples of boosting | Boosting is more prone to overfitting noisy data and needs careful tuning of learning rate and number of rounds

text: How does gradient boosting work, step by step?
ideal_key_points: Starts with a simple initial prediction such as the mean or log-odds | At each round computes the negative gradient of the loss with respect to current predictions, the pseudo-residuals | Fits a shallow tree to these pseudo-residuals | Adds the tree to the ensemble scaled by a learning rate or shrinkage factor | Repeats for many rounds, with early stopping on validation to choose the number of trees

text: Explain how an SVM works and what the kernel trick does.
ideal_key_points: SVM finds the hyperplane that maximizes the margin between classes | Only the support vectors, the points closest to the boundary, define the hyperplane | Soft margin with parameter C trades off margin width against misclassification | Kernel trick computes inner products in a high-dimensional feature space without explicitly mapping, enabling non-linear boundaries | Common kernels are linear, polynomial and RBF, with gamma controlling RBF width

text: What are the main differences between XGBoost and LightGBM?
ideal_key_points: Both are gradient boosted tree libraries with regularization and support for missing values | LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise, XGBoost by default grows level-wise or depth-wise | LightGBM uses histogram binning plus GOSS and exclusive feature bundling for speed and lower memory | LightGBM is usually faster on large datasets but leaf-wise growth can overfit small data, controlled by num_leaves | LightGBM has native categorical feature handling, XGBoost added it later

text: What are the limitations of k-means, and when would you choose DBSCAN or a Gaussian mixture model instead?
ideal_key_points: k-means assumes roughly spherical, similarly sized clusters and needs k in advance | It is sensitive to initialization, mitigated by k-means++, and to outliers and feature scale | DBSCAN finds arbitrarily shaped clusters based on density, labels noise points and does not need k | Gaussian mixture models allow elliptical clusters and give soft probabilistic assignments | DBSCAN struggles with varying densities and needs eps and min_samples tuning

text: Why does kNN struggle with high-dimensional data, and how would you mitigate it?
ideal_key_points: Curse of dimensionality, distances between points become nearly equal so nearest neighbors are not meaningfully near | Data becomes sparse and you need exponentially more samples to cover the space | Irrelevant and unscaled features dominate distance calculations | Mitigate with feature scaling, feature selection, dimensionality reduction such as PCA or learned embeddings | For large datasets use approximate nearest neighbor indexes like KD-trees, HNSW or FAISS

text: How do the regularization terms and hyperparameters in XGBoost control overfitting?
ideal_key_points: Objective includes a penalty on number of leaves via gamma and on leaf weights via L2 lambda and L1 alpha | max_depth and min_child_weight limit tree complexity | Learning rate eta shrinks each tree contribution, used with more rounds and early stopping | subsample and colsample_bytree add row and column randomness | Split is made only if gain exceeds gamma, which prunes weak splits

text: Design a credit card fraud detection system for a bank processing millions of transactions per day.
ideal_key_points: Real-time scoring path with tight latency, e.g. under 100 ms, plus a rules layer for known patterns | Features include transaction amount, merchant, location, device and velocity aggregates like count of transactions in the last hour, served from a feature store | Handles extreme class imbalance with appropriate metrics like PR-AUC and recall at fixed false positive rate, plus class weights or resampling | Gradient boosted trees as a strong baseline, possibly graph or sequence features, with threshold tuned to business cost of fraud versus false declines | Delayed and noisy labels from chargebacks, drift monitoring, adversarial adaptation and regular retraining with a human review loop

text: What is a confusion matrix?
ideal_key_points: A table comparing predicted classes against actual classes | For binary classification it contains true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives | Metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall and specificity are derived from it | Shows which types of errors the model makes, not just how many

text: Define precision and recall.
ideal_key_points: Precision is TP divided by TP plus FP, of predicted positives how many are correct | Recall is TP divided by TP plus FN, of actual positives how many were found | There is a trade-off controlled by the decision threshold | Example where precision matters, like spam filtering, and where recall matters, like cancer screening

text: What is accuracy, and when is it a misleading metric?
ideal_key_points: Accuracy is correct predictions divided by total predictions | Misleading on imbalanced data, e.g. 99 percent accuracy by always predicting the majority class when only 1 percent are positive | Ignores the different costs of false positives and false negatives | Use precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC or balanced accuracy instead

text: What is k-fold cross-validation?
ideal_key_points: Split the data into k equal folds | Train on k minus 1 folds and validate on the remaining fold, rotating k times | Average the k scores for a more reliable performance estimate | Uses all data for both training and validation, useful for small datasets | Common values are k equal to 5 or 10, at the cost of k times the training

text: What is the F1 score and why is it the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic mean?
ideal_key_points: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2PR divided by P plus R | Harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller value, so a model cannot score high by maximizing only one of them | E.g. precision 1.0 and recall 0.0 gives F1 of 0 but an arithmetic mean of 0.5 | F-beta generalizes it to weight recall more or less than precision | For multiclass, macro, micro and weighted averaging differ

text: What does ROC-AUC measure?
ideal_key_points: ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate across all thresholds | AUC is the area under that curve, 0.5 is random and 1.0 is perfect | Equivalent to the probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative | It is threshold independent and measures ranking quality, not calibration

text: Which regression metrics do you know, and how do MAE and RMSE differ?
ideal_key_points: Names MAE, MSE, RMSE, R squared and MAPE | MAE averages absolute errors and is robust to outliers | RMSE squares errors before averaging, so it penalizes large errors more heavily | Both are in the units of the target, unlike MSE | MAPE breaks down when actual values are near zero, R squared measures variance explained

text: What is data leakage? Give an example.
ideal_key_points: Leakage is when information unavailable at prediction time is used in training, inflating validation scores | Target leakage example, a feature derived from the outcome such as a refund flag when predicting fraud | Train-test contamination example, fitting a scaler or imputer on the full dataset before splitting | Temporal leakage, using future data to predict the past, or duplicates across train and test | Symptom is suspiciously high validation performance that collapses in production

text: When would you use stratified k-fold cross-validation?
ideal_key_points: Stratified k-fold keeps the class proportions in each fold the same as in the full dataset | Important for imbalanced classification so each fold contains enough minority examples | Reduces variance of the performance estimate across folds | Use group k-fold instead when samples from the same user or patient must not span train and validation

text: How would you choose the classification threshold for a model?
ideal_key_points: Default 0.5 is arbitrary and often not optimal | Choose based on business costs of false positives versus false negatives | Use the precision-recall curve or ROC curve on a validation set, e.g. maximize F1 or meet a minimum recall | Threshold must be tuned on validation data, not the test set | Threshold may need recalibration if the class prior changes in production

text: Compare ROC-AUC and PR-AUC. When would you prefer PR-AUC?
ideal_key_points: ROC-AUC uses TPR and FPR, PR-AUC uses precision and recall | With heavy imbalance FPR stays small because true negatives are huge, so ROC-AUC can look optimistic | PR-AUC focuses on performance on the positive class and is sensitive to false positives | Random baseline for PR-AUC equals the positive class prevalence, while for ROC-AUC it is 0.5 | Prefer PR-AUC for rare-event problems like fraud, defect or disease detection

text: How do you handle a heavily imbalanced dataset, for example 1 percent positives?
ideal_key_points: Use appropriate metrics like precision, recall, F1 and PR-AUC instead of accuracy | Class weights or a cost-sensitive loss such as focal loss | Resampling, random undersampling of the majority or oversampling such as SMOTE, applied only to training folds | Tune the decision threshold rather than relying on 0.5 | Use stratified splits and consider collecting more minority examples

text: How should you do cross-validation for time series data?
ideal_key_points: Random k-fold leaks future information into training and gives optimistic scores | Use forward chaining or rolling-origin splits where training always precedes validation in time | Options include expanding window and sliding window | Add a gap between train and validation when features use lagged or rolling windows | Final test set should be the most recent period

text: Your model has 99 percent validation accuracy but performs poorly in production. What could be wrong?
ideal_key_points: Data leakage inflating validation results, e.g. target leakage or duplicates across splits | Class imbalance making accuracy misleading | Training-serving skew, features computed differently in production | Distribution shift between historical validation data and live data | Validation split not representative, e.g. random split instead of time-based or group-based

text: What is model calibration, and how would you check and fix it?
ideal_key_points: A calibrated model's predicted probability matches observed frequency, e.g. of predictions at 0.8 about 80 percent are positive | Check with a reliability diagram and metrics like expected calibration error or Brier score | Fix with Platt scaling, isotonic regression or temperature scaling on a held-out calibration set | Boosted trees, SVMs and deep networks are often miscalibrated, logistic regression usually well calibrated | Matters when probabilities drive decisions, such as risk scoring or expected cost

text: Your model has high precision but very low recall on the minority class. What would you try?
ideal_key_points: Lower the decision threshold and check the precision-recall trade-off on validation | Increase minority class weight or use focal loss | Oversample the minority class or undersample the majority in training only | Inspect missed positives for patterns and add features or more labeled data for them | Check for label noise and confirm the business acceptable precision floor

text: How do you do hyperparameter tuning without leaking information into your final performance estimate?
