ideal_key_points: Tuning on the same data used to report performance gives an optimistically biased estimate | Use a separate held-out test set touched only once after tuning | Or use nested cross-validation, inner loop for tuning and outer loop for estimating performance | All preprocessing such as scaling, imputation and feature selection must be fit inside each training fold using a pipeline | Search with grid, random search or Bayesian optimization such as Optuna

text: Design a recommendation system for an e-commerce site, including how you would evaluate it.
ideal_key_points: Two-stage architecture with candidate generation, e.g. collaborative filtering, two-tower embeddings and ANN retrieval, followed by a ranking model | Uses implicit feedback like clicks, add to cart and purchases plus user, item and context features | Handles cold start with content-based features and popularity fallbacks | Offline evaluation with ranking metrics such as recall at k, NDCG and MAP on time-based splits | Online A/B testing on business metrics like CTR, conversion and revenue, with attention to diversity, position bias and feedback loops

text: Why do we scale features, and what is the difference between normalization and standardization?
ideal_key_points: Features on very different scales can dominate distance-based models and slow gradient descent convergence | Normalization or min-max scaling maps values to a fixed range such as 0 to 1 | Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, giving zero mean and unit variance | Min-max is sensitive to outliers, robust scaling using median and IQR helps | Scaler must be fit on training data only

text: What is one-hot encoding?
ideal_key_points: Converts a categorical variable into binary columns, one per category | Exactly one column is 1 for each row | Avoids implying an order that label encoding would introduce | Can blow up dimensionality for high-cardinality features | Dropping one column avoids perfect multicollinearity in linear models

text: What are common ways to handle missing values?
ideal_key_points: Drop rows or columns when missingness is small or the column is mostly empty | Impute with mean, median or mode | Model-based imputation such as kNN or iterative imputation | Add a missing indicator flag since missingness can be informative | Some models like XGBoost and LightGBM handle missing values natively

text: Which algorithms are sensitive to feature scaling and which are not?
ideal_key_points: Distance-based methods like kNN, k-means and SVM with RBF kernel are sensitive | Gradient-descent-trained models such as linear models with regularization and neural networks benefit from scaling | PCA is sensitive because it is based on variance | Tree-based models like decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting are largely invariant to monotonic scaling

text: How would you encode a categorical feature with thousands of unique values, like a pincode or product ID?
ideal_key_points: One-hot encoding becomes too high-dimensional and sparse | Target or mean encoding with smoothing and out-of-fold computation | Frequency or count encoding | Hashing trick to a fixed number of buckets | Learned embeddings in neural networks, or grouping rare categories into an other bucket

text: How would you handle outliers in a numeric feature?
ideal_key_points: Detect with IQR rule, z-scores, box plots or isolation forest | First check whether they are data errors or genuine rare values | Options include capping or winsorizing, log or Box-Cox transforms, or removal if erroneous | Use robust scalers or robust losses such as Huber | Tree models are less affected, linear models and distance-based models are strongly affected

text: What is target encoding and how do you prevent it from leaking the target?
ideal_key_points: Replaces each category with the mean of the target for that category | Naively computing it on the full training set leaks the label of each row into its own feature, causing overfitting | Compute it out-of-fold so each row is encoded using other folds only | Apply smoothing toward the global mean for rare categories | Fit encodings on training data only and apply them to validation and test

text: How would you do feature selection on a dataset with hundreds of features?
ideal_key_points: Filter methods such as removing low-variance features, correlation analysis, mutual information or chi-square | Wrapper methods such as recursive feature elimination | Embedded methods such as L1 regularization or tree-based feature importance | Permutation importance or SHAP on a validation set as more reliable importance measures | Perform selection inside cross-validation folds to avoid leakage

text: What features would you engineer from a timestamp column?
ideal_key_points: Calendar components like hour, day of week, month, weekend and holiday flags, including Indian festivals where relevant | Cyclical encoding with sine and cosine so hour 23 is close to hour 0 | Time since an event, e.g. time since last purchase or account age | Lag and rolling window aggregates computed only from past data | Handle time zones consistently

text: How would you decide whether values are missing at random, and why does it matter for imputation?
ideal_key_points: Distinguishes MCAR, missing completely at random, MAR, missing at random given observed data, and MNAR, missing not at random | Investigate by comparing distributions of other features and the target between rows with and without missing values | Simple mean imputation is reasonable mainly under MCAR and can bias results otherwise | Under MAR use model-based or multiple imputation conditioned on observed features | Under MNAR the missingness itself carries signal, so add an indicator feature and consult domain experts

text: Design a real-time feature pipeline for a ride ETA prediction model, keeping training and serving consistent.
ideal_key_points: Batch features like historical average speed per road segment and time slot computed offline | Streaming features like current traffic, recent trip durations and driver location computed with Kafka plus Flink or Spark Streaming | A feature store with offline and online stores so the same feature definitions serve training and inference | Point-in-time correct joins for training data to avoid leakage from future values | Low latency online lookup, freshness monitoring, default values for missing features and checks for training-serving skew

text: What is an activation function and why do we need non-linearity?
ideal_key_points: Activation functions are applied to each neuron's weighted sum | Without non-linearity a stack of linear layers collapses into a single linear transformation | Non-linearity lets networks approximate complex functions | Examples include ReLU, sigmoid, tanh and GELU

text: What is an epoch, a batch and an iteration?
ideal_key_points: An epoch is one full pass through the training dataset | A batch is a subset of samples processed together in one forward and backward pass | An iteration or step is one parameter update, processing one batch | Iterations per epoch equals dataset size divided by batch size

text: What is dropout?
ideal_key_points: Regularization technique that randomly sets a fraction of activations to zero during training | Prevents co-adaptation of neurons and acts like training an ensemble of sub-networks | Typical rates are 0.1 to 0.5 | Disabled at inference, with scaling by keep probability, usually done during training as inverted dropout

text: Compare ReLU, sigmoid and tanh activations.
ideal_key_points: Sigmoid outputs 0 to 1 and saturates at both ends, causing vanishing gradients, and is not zero-centered | Tanh outputs minus 1 to 1, is zero-centered but still saturates | ReLU outputs max of 0 and x, is cheap and does not saturate for positive inputs, which helps deep networks train | ReLU can suffer from dying neurons stuck at zero, fixed by Leaky ReLU, ELU or GELU | Sigmoid is still used for binary output layers and gates

text: What is backpropagation?
ideal_key_points: Algorithm to compute gradients of the loss with respect to all weights | Forward pass computes activations and the loss | Backward pass applies the chain rule layer by layer from output to input | Reuses intermediate results so the cost is similar to a forward pass | The gradients are then used by an optimizer such as SGD or Adam to update weights

text: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
ideal_key_points: Gradients shrink exponentially as they are multiplied through many layers or time steps | Early layers learn very slowly or not at all | Caused by saturating activations like sigmoid and tanh and by poor weight initialization | Mitigated with ReLU, proper initialization like He or Xavier, batch normalization, residual connections, and LSTM or GRU for sequences

text: What is batch normalization and why does it help?
ideal_key_points: Normalizes each feature in a layer using the mini-batch mean and variance | Then applies learnable scale gamma and shift beta | Allows higher learning rates, faster and more stable training, and reduces sensitivity to initialization | Has a mild regularizing effect from batch noise | Uses running averages of mean and variance at inference, so train and eval modes differ

text: What is transfer learning and when would you use it?
ideal_key_points: Reusing a model pretrained on a large dataset, like ImageNet or a large text corpus, for a new task | Either use it as a frozen feature extractor or fine-tune some or all layers | Useful when the target dataset is small or compute is limited | Works best when source and target domains are related | Usually replace the final head and use a lower learning rate for pretrained layers

text: What is softmax and why is it paired with cross-entropy loss?
ideal_key_points: Softmax converts a vector of logits into a probability distribution that sums to 1 by exponentiating and normalizing | Cross-entropy measures the negative log probability of the correct class | Combined, the gradient with respect to logits simplifies to predicted probability minus the one-hot target | Frameworks fuse them, e.g. log-softmax, for numerical stability, so you pass raw logits to the loss

text: How do LSTMs address the vanishing gradient problem in RNNs?
ideal_key_points: Plain RNNs multiply gradients by the recurrent weight matrix at each step, so they vanish or explode over long sequences | LSTMs add a cell state that is updated additively, giving a near-linear path for gradients | Forget, input and output gates control what is erased, written and exposed | When the forget gate is near 1 information and gradients persist across many time steps | Gates use sigmoid and candidate values use tanh

text: Compare LSTM and GRU.
ideal_key_points: LSTM has three gates, forget, input and output, plus a separate cell state | GRU has two gates, update and reset, and merges cell and hidden state | GRU has fewer parameters and trains faster | Performance is often similar, LSTM may do better on longer or more complex dependencies | Choice is usually empirical, both largely replaced by transformers for many NLP tasks

text: How do you deal with exploding gradients?
ideal_key_points: Symptoms are loss spikes, NaN values and very large weight updates | Gradient clipping by global norm or by value | Lower the learning rate or use warmup | Proper weight initialization and normalization layers | Use gated architectures or residual connections, and check for bad input data or division by zero in the loss

text: Explain the attention mechanism in transformers.
ideal_key_points: Each token is projected into query, key and value vectors | Attention scores are dot products of the query with all keys, scaled and passed through softmax | Output is the weighted sum of values, so each token can attend to every other token | Multi-head attention runs several attention heads in parallel to capture different relationships | Unlike RNNs it processes all positions in parallel and captures long-range dependencies directly

text: Why are weight initialization schemes like Xavier and He important?
ideal_key_points: Bad initialization causes activations and gradients to vanish or explode as they pass through layers | All-zero initialization makes neurons symmetric so they learn identical features | Xavier or Glorot initialization scales variance by fan-in and fan-out, suited to tanh and sigmoid | He initialization uses variance 2 divided by fan-in, suited to ReLU | Goal is to keep activation variance roughly constant across layers

text: Why do transformers use scaled dot-product attention, dividing by the square root of the key dimension?
ideal_key_points: For random vectors the variance of the dot product grows linearly with the dimension d_k | Large logits push softmax into saturated regions where one weight is near 1 | Saturated softmax produces very small gradients and unstable training | Dividing by the square root of d_k keeps the logits at roughly unit variance

text: Compare batch normalization and layer normalization, and explain why transformers use layer norm.
ideal_key_points: Batch norm normalizes each feature across the batch, layer norm normalizes across features within each single example | Batch norm depends on batch statistics, so it struggles with small batches and variable-length sequences and behaves differently at train and inference | Layer norm is independent of batch size and identical at train and inference | Transformers use layer norm, often pre-norm or RMSNorm, for stable training on padded variable-length sequences | Batch norm remains common in CNNs

text: What is the role of positional encoding in transformers, and what alternatives exist?
ideal_key_points: Self-attention is permutation invariant, so without position information word order is lost | Original transformer added fixed sinusoidal encodings of different frequencies to the embeddings | Learned absolute position embeddings are used in BERT and GPT-2 | Relative schemes such as rotary embeddings RoPE and ALiBi encode relative distance | Relative methods generally extrapolate better to longer sequences

text: When fine-tuning a pretrained model, how do you decide which layers to freeze and what learning rate to use?
ideal_key_points: Small dataset similar to the source, freeze most layers and train only the head | Larger dataset or a different domain, unfreeze more layers or the whole network | Early layers learn generic features, later layers are more task specific | Use a lower learning rate for pretrained layers than the new head, discriminative learning rates, and possibly gradual unfreezing | Watch for catastrophic forgetting and consider parameter-efficient methods like LoRA or adapters

text: Explain why self-attention is quadratic in sequence length and what techniques reduce that cost.
ideal_key_points: Attention computes a score for every pair of tokens, so compute and memory scale with n squared | Long contexts become dominated by attention memory | FlashAttention keeps exact attention but tiles computation in on-chip SRAM to avoid materializing the n by n matrix, cutting memory to linear | Sparse or local windowed attention, linear attention approximations and low-rank methods reduce complexity at some quality cost | At inference KV caching avoids recomputing past keys and values, with grouped-query attention shrinking the cache

text: Your loss becomes NaN halfway through training a large model with mixed precision. How would you debug it?
ideal_key_points: Check for exploding gradients by logging gradient norms and add gradient clipping | FP16 overflow or underflow, ensure dynamic loss scaling is enabled or switch to bf16 | Lower the learning rate or extend warmup, and check the scheduler | Look for numerically unsafe operations like log of zero, division by zero or softmax without max subtraction, keeping those in fp32 | Find the offending batch and inspect data for corrupt or extreme values, resuming from the last good checkpoint

text: What is a convolution in a CNN?
ideal_key_points: A small learnable filter or kernel slides over the image computing dot products with local patches | Produces a feature map that detects patterns like edges or textures | Weights are shared across spatial positions, reducing parameters | Hyperparameters include kernel size, stride, padding and number of filters

text: What is pooling and why is it used?
ideal_key_points: Pooling downsamples feature maps, e.g. max pooling takes the maximum in each window | Reduces spatial size, computation and parameters in later layers | Provides some translation invariance | Global average pooling is often used before the classifier head

text: Why are CNNs better than fully connected networks for images?
ideal_key_points: Local connectivity exploits spatial structure, nearby pixels are related | Weight sharing drastically reduces the number of parameters | Translation equivariance, the same feature is detected anywhere in the image | Hierarchical features, early layers detect edges and deeper layers detect parts and objects | Fully connected layers on raw pixels have huge parameter counts and overfit

text: What image augmentation techniques do you know and when can they hurt?
ideal_key_points: Geometric augmentations like flips, rotations, random crops and scaling | Photometric augmentations like brightness, contrast, color jitter, blur and noise | Advanced methods like Cutout, MixUp and CutMix | Augmentations must preserve the label, e.g. flipping digits like 6 and 9 or text, or rotating in medical images can change meaning | For detection and segmentation the boxes and masks must be transformed too, and augmentation is applied only to training data

text: What preprocessing steps would you do with OpenCV before feeding images to a model?
ideal_key_points: Read the image and convert BGR to RGB since OpenCV loads in BGR order | Resize to the model input size, possibly with letterboxing to keep aspect ratio | Convert to float, scale to 0 to 1 and normalize with the same mean and std used in training | Rearrange from HWC to CHW layout for PyTorch and add a batch dimension | Optional steps like denoising, histogram equalization or CLAHE, cropping regions of interest or face detection

text: What is the difference between image classification, object detection and segmentation?
ideal_key_points: Classification assigns one label to the whole image | Object detection finds objects with bounding boxes and class labels | Semantic segmentation labels every pixel with a class | Instance segmentation also separates individual objects of the same class, e.g. Mask R-CNN | Each needs progressively more detailed annotations

text: Explain IoU and non-maximum suppression in object detection.
ideal_key_points: IoU is the area of overlap divided by the area of union of two boxes | IoU thresholds decide whether a prediction matches ground truth, e.g. 0.5, and are used in mAP | Detectors output many overlapping boxes for the same object | NMS keeps the highest-confidence box and removes others with IoU above a threshold, per class | Soft-NMS decays scores instead of removing boxes to help with crowded scenes

text: Compare one-stage detectors like YOLO with two-stage detectors like Faster R-CNN.
ideal_key_points: Two-stage detectors first propose regions with a region proposal network, then classify and refine each region | One-stage detectors predict boxes and classes directly in a single pass over a grid or anchors | One-stage detectors are faster and suit real-time applications | Two-stage detectors historically had higher accuracy, especially for small objects, though modern YOLO versions narrow the gap | Mentions anchors versus anchor-free designs or the mAP versus FPS trade-off

text: How would you build a video classification model using a CNN combined with an LSTM?
ideal_key_points: Sample a fixed number of frames per clip | Pass each frame through a pretrained CNN, often frozen, to get a feature vector per frame | Feed the sequence of frame features into an LSTM or GRU to model temporal dynamics | Classify from the final hidden state or pooled hidden states | Alternatives include 3D CNNs, two-stream networks with optical flow, or video transformers

text: What are residual connections, and why did they let ResNet train very deep networks?
ideal_key_points: A residual block outputs F of x plus x, learning a residual instead of a full mapping | The identity shortcut gives gradients a direct path backward, reducing vanishing gradients | Solves the degradation problem where deeper plain networks had higher training error | Easy for a block to learn identity by driving F to zero, so extra depth does not hurt | A 1 by 1 convolution projection is used when dimensions change, and the idea is now used in transformers too

text: Design a real-time deepfake detection pipeline for video calls.
ideal_key_points: Pipeline of frame sampling, face detection and alignment, then a per-face classifier such as EfficientNet or a ViT | Temporal modeling across frames to catch flicker and inconsistencies, plus possible audio-visual sync checks | Latency budget met by sampling frames, lightweight models, quantization and GPU or edge inference, aggregating scores over a sliding window | Training data from diverse generation methods with heavy augmentation for compression, and evaluation on unseen generators for generalization | Threshold tuned for low false positives, calibrated confidence, human review, drift monitoring and frequent retraining as new deepfake methods appear

text: Design a system to detect defects on a factory assembly line using cameras, when you have very few labeled defect images.
ideal_key_points: Controlled image capture with fixed lighting and camera position to reduce variance | Use anomaly detection trained on normal images only, e.g. autoencoders or feature-embedding methods like PatchCore | Transfer learning from pretrained backbones plus heavy augmentation and possibly synthetic defects | Edge deployment with latency matching line speed, using quantized models | Recall-focused thresholding, human-in-the-loop review of flagged items, and active learning to grow the labeled defect set

text: What is tokenization?
ideal_key_points: Splitting text into units called tokens that a model processes | Tokens can be words, subwords or characters | Each token is mapped to an integer ID from a vocabulary | Choice of tokenizer affects vocabulary size, sequence length and handling of unknown words

text: What are stop words, and what is the difference between stemming and lemmatization?
ideal_key_points: Stop words are very common words like the, is and and that are often removed in classical NLP | Stemming chops word endings with rules, e.g. studies to studi, and may produce non-words | Lemmatization maps words to their dictionary form using vocabulary and part of speech, e.g. better to good | These steps help bag-of-words models but are usually unnecessary for transformers

text: What are word embeddings, and how is Word2Vec trained?
ideal_key_points: Dense low-dimensional vectors representing words, where similar words have nearby vectors | Word2Vec learns from context in a shallow network | Skip-gram predicts context words from the center word, CBOW predicts the center word from context | Uses negative sampling or hierarchical softmax for efficiency | Embeddings capture analogies like king minus man plus woman close to queen

text: What is TF-IDF?
ideal_key_points: Term frequency counts how often a term appears in a document | Inverse document frequency downweights terms that appear in many documents, typically log of N divided by document frequency | Score is TF multiplied by IDF, highlighting terms distinctive to a document | Produces sparse vectors used for search and classification with linear models | Ignores word order and semantics

text: Why do modern models use subword tokenization like BPE or WordPiece?
ideal_key_points: Word-level vocabularies are huge and cannot handle unseen words | Character-level tokenization makes sequences very long | Subword methods split rare words into frequent pieces, so there are effectively no out-of-vocabulary words | BPE iteratively merges the most frequent symbol pairs, WordPiece merges based on likelihood | Works across languages and morphology, though some languages like Indic scripts may need more tokens per word

text: Compare BERT and GPT in terms of architecture and training objective.
ideal_key_points: BERT is an encoder-only transformer, GPT is a decoder-only transformer | BERT uses bidirectional attention, GPT uses causal masked attention seeing only previous tokens | BERT is pretrained with masked language modeling, GPT with next-token prediction | BERT suits understanding tasks like classification, NER and embeddings | GPT suits generation and is used for prompting and few-shot learning

text: What is the difference between static embeddings like Word2Vec and contextual embeddings like BERT?
ideal_key_points: Static embeddings assign one fixed vector per word regardless of context | Contextual embeddings give each token occurrence a vector based on the whole sentence | Contextual models handle polysemy, e.g. bank in river bank versus bank account | Contextual models are much larger and costlier to run | Sentence-level embeddings often come from pooling or models like Sentence-BERT

text: How would you fine-tune BERT for a text classification task?
ideal_key_points: Tokenize with the matching tokenizer, adding special tokens, padding, truncation and attention masks | Add a classification head on the CLS token or pooled output | Fine-tune end to end with a small learning rate around 2e-5 to 5e-5 for a few epochs using AdamW with warmup | Use a validation set with early stopping and an appropriate metric like F1 | Handle class imbalance and maximum sequence length of 512 tokens

text: Explain how sampling strategies like temperature, top-k and top-p affect text generation.
ideal_key_points: Greedy decoding picks the most likely token and can be repetitive, beam search explores several sequences | Temperature divides logits before softmax, lower makes output more deterministic, higher more random | Top-k samples only from the k most likely tokens | Top-p or nucleus sampling samples from the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds p, adapting to the distribution | Repetition penalties further reduce loops, and low temperature suits factual tasks

text: Design a text classification system for customer complaints written in Hindi, English and Hinglish, with very little labeled data.
ideal_key_points: Use a multilingual pretrained model such as mBERT, XLM-R, MuRIL or IndicBERT | Handle code-mixed and romanized text with normalization or transliteration | Bootstrap labels using LLM zero-shot or few-shot labeling, weak supervision and active learning with human review | Fine-tune and evaluate per language with macro F1 given imbalance | Deploy with confidence thresholds routing uncertain cases to humans and monitor drift

text: Design a semantic search system over a million internal support documents.
ideal_key_points: Chunk documents and compute embeddings with a sentence embedding model | Store vectors in an approximate nearest neighbor index such as FAISS, HNSW or a vector database | Hybrid retrieval combining BM25 keyword search with dense retrieval, followed by a cross-encoder reranker | Evaluate with labeled query-document pairs using recall at k, MRR or NDCG | Handle incremental index updates, metadata filters, access control, latency and caching

text: What is the difference between batch inference and online inference?
ideal_key_points: Batch inference scores large sets of data on a schedule and stores the predictions | Online inference serves predictions on demand via an API with low latency | Batch is cheaper and simpler but predictions can be stale | Online is needed when inputs arrive in real time, e.g. fraud checks or search ranking | Examples of each, like nightly churn scores versus real-time recommendations

text: Why is experiment tracking important, and what tools have you used?
ideal_key_points: Records hyperparameters, code version, data version, metrics and artifacts for each run | Makes results reproducible and comparable | Helps teams avoid repeating experiments and pick the best model | Tools such as MLflow, Weights and Biases, Neptune or TensorBoard

text: Compare TensorFlow and PyTorch.
ideal_key_points: PyTorch uses eager execution by default with a Pythonic, easy to debug style | TensorFlow 2 also defaults to eager with Keras as the high-level API, and tf.function builds graphs | PyTorch dominates research and most new open-source models, including the Hugging Face ecosystem | TensorFlow has mature deployment tooling such as TF Serving, TFLite and TF.js | PyTorch deployment uses TorchScript, torch.compile, ONNX export or TorchServe

text: What is ONNX and why would you export a model to it?
ideal_key_points: ONNX is an open, framework-independent format for representing models as computation graphs | Allows training in one framework like PyTorch and running in another runtime | ONNX Runtime provides optimized inference on CPU and GPU, and works with TensorRT and OpenVINO | Enables graph optimizations and quantization for faster deployment | Need to verify outputs match after export and handle unsupported operators and dynamic axes

text: What is model versioning, and what should be versioned along with the model?
ideal_key_points: Tracking each trained model as an immutable, identifiable version in a model registry | Version the training code via git commit, training data snapshot and preprocessing pipeline | Record hyperparameters, environment and dependency versions and evaluation metrics | Track stage such as staging or production to enable rollback | Tools include MLflow Model Registry and DVC

text: What is data drift versus concept drift, and how would you detect them?
ideal_key_points: Data drift or covariate shift is a change in the input feature distribution | Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and the target | Detect data drift with statistical tests like Kolmogorov-Smirnov, chi-square or population stability index on features and predictions | Detect concept drift by monitoring performance once labels arrive, or using proxies when labels are delayed | Respond with alerts, investigation and retraining on recent data

text: How would you A/B test a new model against the current production model?
ideal_key_points: Randomly split traffic, often by user ID, between the control model and the new model | Define a primary business metric and guardrail metrics like latency and error rates up front | Calculate required sample size and run long enough for statistical significance and weekly cycles | Avoid peeking and novelty effects | Start with shadow mode or a canary rollout before a full A/B test

text: What is quantization, and what are the trade-offs between post-training quantization and quantization-aware training?
ideal_key_points: Quantization represents weights and activations in lower precision, e.g. int8 instead of fp32 | Reduces model size around 4 times and speeds up inference on supporting hardware | Post-training quantization is applied after training, possibly with calibration data, and is quick but may lose accuracy | Quantization-aware training simulates quantization during training so the model adapts, giving better accuracy at more cost | Dynamic versus static quantization, and LLM methods like 4-bit GPTQ or AWQ

text: What is training-serving skew, and how do you prevent it?
ideal_key_points: Model performance in production differs from offline because the input data or features differ | Causes include different feature code paths in training and serving, different preprocessing, or stale or missing features | Prevent by sharing the same transformation code or packaging preprocessing with the model | Use a feature store and point-in-time correct training data | Log serving features and compare their distributions against training data

text: Design a model monitoring setup for a production ML model.
ideal_key_points: Monitor system metrics like latency, throughput, error rate and resource usage | Log inputs, predictions and model version for each request | Monitor data quality and drift in features and prediction distributions with metrics like PSI | Join delayed ground truth labels to track real performance metrics over time and by segment | Dashboards and alerting with thresholds, plus a runbook for rollback or retraining, using tools like Prometheus, Grafana or Evidently

text: Design an end-to-end ML pipeline that automatically retrains and redeploys a model when its performance drops.
ideal_key_points: Triggers based on monitored performance degradation, drift thresholds or a schedule | Automated pipeline for data extraction, validation, feature computation, training and evaluation, orchestrated with Airflow, Kubeflow or similar | Gate deployment by comparing the candidate against the current model on a fixed holdout and recent data | Register versioned models and roll out via shadow or canary deployment with automatic rollback | Guard against training on corrupted or feedback-loop data and keep humans in the loop for approval

text: Design a system to serve a deep learning model to millions of users with p99 latency under 100 milliseconds.
ideal_key_points: Containerized model servers like Triton, TorchServe or TF Serving behind a load balancer with autoscaling | Optimize the model with ONNX or TensorRT, quantization, distillation or pruning | Dynamic batching to improve GPU throughput within the latency budget | Caching of frequent predictions and precomputed features, with a fast online feature store | Monitor p99 latency, use timeouts and fallback models, and load test before launch

text: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python, and when would you use each?
ideal_key_points: Lists are mutable while tuples are immutable | Tuples are hashable when all their elements are hashable, so they can be dict keys or set members | Tuples are slightly smaller in memory and faster to create | Use tuples for fixed records like coordinates or return values and lists for collections that grow or change

text: What does it mean for a Python object to be mutable or immutable? Give a few examples of each.
ideal_key_points: Mutable objects can be changed in place after creation | Examples of mutable types are list, dict, set and bytearray | Examples of immutable types are int, float, str, tuple and frozenset | Modifying an immutable value actually creates a new object with a new id | Only immutable or hashable objects can be used as dict keys

text: What is the difference between the is operator and the double-equals operator in Python?
ideal_key_points: is checks identity, meaning both names point to the same object in memory | Double-equals checks value equality by calling __eq__ | Use is for singletons such as None, True and False | Small integer caching and string interning can make is appear to work for values, so it should not be relied on for equality

text: What is a generator in Python, and how is it different from a function that returns a list?
ideal_key_points: A generator function uses yield and produces values lazily one at a time | It keeps its local state between calls to next | It uses constant memory instead of building the whole list up front | A generator can only be iterated once and raises StopIteration when exhausted | Generator expressions use parentheses instead of square brackets

text: Explain the mutable default argument pitfall in Python and how you would avoid it.
ideal_key_points: Default argument values are evaluated once when the function is defined, not on every call | A mutable default like a list or dict is therefore shared across all calls | Mutations from one call leak into later calls | Fix by using None as the default and creating a new object inside the function

text: Compare the time complexity of checking membership in a list, a set and a dict. Why the difference?
ideal_key_points: Membership in a list is O(n) because it scans linearly | Sets and dicts use hash tables, giving average O(1) lookups | Worst case for hash lookups degrades to O(n) with many collisions | Elements of sets and keys of dicts must be hashable | Converting a list to a set is worthwhile when doing many lookups

text: What is the difference between an iterable and an iterator in Python?
ideal_key_points: An iterable implements __iter__ and returns a new iterator, for example a list | An iterator implements __next__ and its __iter__ returns itself | An iterator raises StopIteration when there are no more items | A for loop calls iter on the iterable and then next repeatedly | A list is iterable but not an iterator, so it can be looped over many times

text: What is a decorator in Python? Walk me through how you would write one that logs how long a function takes.
ideal_key_points: A decorator is a callable that takes a function and returns a new function, usually a wrapper | The @decorator syntax is shorthand for func = decorator(func) | The wrapper accepts *args and **kwargs and calls the original function | Measure time with time.perf_counter before and after the call | Use functools.wraps to preserve the original name and docstring

text: What is a context manager in Python and how would you implement your own?
ideal_key_points: A context manager is used with the with statement to guarantee setup and cleanup | Implement it as a class with __enter__ and __exit__ methods | __exit__ receives exception details and returning True suppresses the exception | contextlib.contextmanager lets you write one as a generator with yield inside try and finally | Common uses are files, locks, database sessions and transactions

text: Explain the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy in Python.
ideal_key_points: A shallow copy creates a new outer container but shares references to the nested objects | copy.copy, slicing and list() produce shallow copies | copy.deepcopy recursively copies nested objects | Mutating a nested object in a shallow copy affects the original | deepcopy uses a memo dictionary to handle shared references and cycles

text: Python type hints are not enforced at runtime. So what does a library like Pydantic add on top of them?
ideal_key_points: The interpreter ignores type hints at runtime; static checkers like mypy or pyright use them | Pydantic reads the annotations and validates data at runtime | It coerces compatible input, for example the string 5 into an int, unless strict mode is used | Invalid data raises a ValidationError with per-field error details | Pydantic v2 has a Rust core and uses model_validate and model_dump

text: How would you write a decorator that takes arguments, for example a retry decorator with a configurable number of attempts?
ideal_key_points: It needs three levels: a factory that takes the arguments, which returns the decorator, which returns the wrapper | The arguments are captured in a closure | The wrapper loops up to max attempts, catching only specific exception types | It re-raises the last exception after the final attempt | Add a delay or exponential backoff between attempts and use functools.wraps

text: What are dunder methods, and which ones would you implement so a custom class supports len, equality comparison and use as a dictionary key?
ideal_key_points: Dunder methods are special methods Python calls for built-in operations, part of the data model | __len__ supports len and __eq__ supports equality | __hash__ is needed for use as a dict key or in a set | Defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes instances unhashable | Objects that compare equal must have equal hashes, so hash only immutable fields

text: Explain how CPython manages memory, including reference counting and the garbage collector. Why might a long-running Python service still grow in memory?
ideal_key_points: CPython frees an object immediately when its reference count drops to zero | A generational cyclic garbage collector finds and frees reference cycles that refcounting cannot | The gc module exposes generations, thresholds and manual collection | Small objects come from pymalloc arenas, and freed memory is not always returned to the OS | Growth often comes from unbounded caches, global lists, lingering references or C extension leaks, which tracemalloc can help find

text: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
ideal_key_points: Concurrency means making progress on multiple tasks by interleaving them | Parallelism means executing multiple tasks at the same instant on multiple cores | asyncio gives concurrency on a single thread without parallelism | Multiprocessing gives true parallelism in Python

text: What is the Global Interpreter Lock in Python and how does it affect multithreaded programs?
ideal_key_points: The GIL is a mutex in CPython that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time | CPU-bound pure Python threads get no parallel speedup | The GIL is released during blocking I/O and by many C extensions like NumPy, so I/O-bound threading still helps | Multiprocessing sidesteps the GIL by using separate processes | Python 3.13 introduced an optional free-threaded build without the GIL

text: What is a race condition, and how would you prevent one in Python?
ideal_key_points: A race condition is when the result depends on the unpredictable interleaving of operations on shared state | Operations like counter += 1 are not atomic across threads | Protect critical sections with threading.Lock, typically using a with block | In asyncio, races can happen across await points and asyncio.Lock is used | Avoiding shared mutable state, for example with queues, is often the cleanest fix

text: What is a deadlock and how can you avoid it?
ideal_key_points: A deadlock is when two or more threads each wait for a lock the other holds, so none can proceed | It requires mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait | Always acquire locks in a consistent global order | Use timeouts when acquiring locks and keep critical sections small | Databases can also deadlock between transactions and will abort one of them

text: Compare threading, multiprocessing and asyncio in Python. When would you choose each?
ideal_key_points: Threading suits I/O-bound work with blocking libraries, shares memory, but is limited by the GIL for CPU work | Multiprocessing suits CPU-bound work, uses separate processes with their own memory and pays pickling and IPC overhead | asyncio uses a single-threaded event loop with cooperative scheduling, ideal for thousands of concurrent network calls | asyncio needs async-compatible libraries throughout | concurrent.futures offers ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor as a common interface

text: What happens if you call blocking code like time.sleep or the requests library inside an async FastAPI endpoint, and how would you fix it?
ideal_key_points: Blocking calls freeze the event loop, so every other request on that worker stalls | Replace with async equivalents such as asyncio.sleep and httpx.AsyncClient | Offload unavoidable blocking calls with asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor | Alternatively declare the endpoint with plain def so FastAPI runs it in a threadpool

text: You need to call an external LLM API for 1000 prompts as fast as possible without getting rate-limited. How would you do it with asyncio?
ideal_key_points: Create tasks for all prompts and run them concurrently with gather or a TaskGroup | Use an asyncio.Semaphore to cap the number of in-flight requests | Retry on 429 and 5xx errors with exponential backoff and jitter, respecting Retry-After | Set per-request timeouts | Reuse a single async HTTP client with a connection pool

text: Explain how the asyncio event loop works. What actually happens when a coroutine hits an await?
ideal_key_points: Calling an async function returns a coroutine object that does not run until awaited or scheduled as a task | The event loop runs ready tasks and uses OS readiness APIs like epoll or kqueue via selectors to watch sockets | At an await on a pending future the coroutine suspends and yields control back to the loop | When the future completes, the loop schedules the task to resume where it left off | Everything runs on one thread, so scheduling is cooperative, not preemptive

text: Compare asyncio.create_task, asyncio.gather and TaskGroup. How do they differ in error handling?
ideal_key_points: create_task schedules a coroutine to run concurrently and returns a Task | gather awaits several awaitables and returns results in input order | By default gather propagates the first exception but does not cancel the others, unless return_exceptions is used | TaskGroup, added in Python 3.11, gives structured concurrency and cancels sibling tasks when one fails, raising an ExceptionGroup | Keep a reference to fire-and-forget tasks so they are not garbage collected

text: Your FastAPI service runs a CPU-heavy model inference inside an async endpoint and latency spikes for all users. Why, and how would you fix it?
ideal_key_points: CPU-bound work in an async endpoint blocks the event loop so no other requests progress | asyncio.to_thread helps only if the library releases the GIL, as PyTorch and NumPy largely do | A ProcessPoolExecutor or multiple worker processes give real parallelism | For heavier loads move inference to a separate model server or worker queue | Batching requests improves GPU or CPU throughput

text: How does task cancellation work in asyncio, and how should you handle cleanup correctly?
ideal_key_points: task.cancel causes CancelledError to be raised inside the coroutine at its next await | Put cleanup in try and finally or catch CancelledError, then re-raise it | Swallowing CancelledError breaks timeouts, TaskGroups and graceful shutdown | asyncio.timeout and wait_for work by cancelling the inner task | asyncio.shield protects an inner operation from outer cancellation

text: What is REST, and what are its key principles?
ideal_key_points: Resources are identified by URLs | Standard HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE act on resources | Requests are stateless, carrying all needed context | Resources are exchanged as representations, usually JSON | Responses should declare cacheability and the interface is uniform

text: What is the difference between POST, PUT and PATCH?
ideal_key_points: POST typically creates a new resource and is not idempotent | PUT replaces the entire resource at a known URL and is idempotent | PATCH applies a partial update to a resource | PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent

text: How does FastAPI validate incoming request data, and what happens when validation fails?
ideal_key_points: Parameters declared with type hints and Pydantic models are validated automatically | FastAPI infers whether a parameter comes from the path, query or body | Invalid input returns a 422 Unprocessable Entity response with field-level error details | response_model validates and filters outgoing data | Schemas are used to generate OpenAPI docs automatically

text: Explain what common HTTP status codes mean, especially 401 versus 403 and 400 versus 422.
ideal_key_points: 200 is OK, 201 is Created and 204 is No Content | 401 means not authenticated, while 403 means authenticated but not allowed | 400 is a malformed request, while 422 means well-formed but semantically invalid, which FastAPI uses for validation errors | 404 is not found, 409 is conflict and 429 is too many requests | 500 is an internal server error and 503 means service unavailable

text: How does dependency injection work in FastAPI, and what would you use it for?
ideal_key_points: Dependencies are declared with Depends in endpoint parameters | FastAPI resolves them per request, supports nesting, and caches each dependency within a request | Dependencies using yield provide setup and teardown, such as opening and closing a DB session | Typical uses are DB sessions, authentication, current user and shared query parameters | app.dependency_overrides lets you swap dependencies in tests

text: How would you design consistent error handling for a FastAPI application?
ideal_key_points: Raise HTTPException with an appropriate status code and detail for expected errors | Register custom exception handlers for domain exceptions | Return a consistent error schema such as code, message and request ID | Never leak stack traces or internal details to clients | Log full error details server-side with the request ID for correlation

text: What does idempotency mean for an API, and how would you make a payment creation endpoint idempotent?
ideal_key_points: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether it runs once or many times | GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition while POST is not | The client sends a unique Idempotency-Key header with the request | The server stores the key with the result and returns the stored response on retries | Enforce uniqueness with a DB constraint and expire keys after a TTL

text: Compare offset-based and cursor-based pagination. When would you use each?
ideal_key_points: Offset pagination uses limit and offset, is simple and allows jumping to a page | Large offsets are slow because the database still scans the skipped rows | Inserts or deletes between pages cause duplicated or skipped items with offsets | Cursor or keyset pagination filters with something like WHERE id greater than the last seen id using an indexed sort key | Cursors are stable and fast but do not support jumping to arbitrary pages

text: When would you use FastAPI's BackgroundTasks versus a proper task queue like Celery?
ideal_key_points: BackgroundTasks run in the same process after the response is sent | They are not persisted, so they are lost if the process crashes, and have no retries | They suit small, quick jobs like sending an email or writing an audit log | Celery or similar queues run in separate workers with durability, retries and scaling | Long or CPU-heavy work belongs in a queue so it does not starve the API

text: You want to stream LLM tokens to a web client as they are generated. Compare polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSockets for this.
ideal_key_points: Polling is simple but adds latency and wasted requests | Server-Sent Events push one-way server-to-client over plain HTTP using text/event-stream, with automatic reconnect | SSE is usually the best fit for token streaming, which is one-directional | WebSockets are full-duplex and suit bidirectional interactive use, but are stateful and harder to scale | Proxies and load balancers must not buffer the response and need suitable timeouts

text: How would you load a large ML model once when a FastAPI app starts rather than on every request?
ideal_key_points: Use the lifespan context manager to run startup and shutdown logic | Load the model at startup and store it on app.state or a module-level holder | Loading per request would add huge latency and memory churn | Each worker process loads its own copy, so memory scales with worker count | Release resources at shutdown and expose a readiness check that passes only after loading

text: An API endpoint that used to take 100 milliseconds now takes 3 seconds in production. Walk me through how you would debug it.
ideal_key_points: Measure first using logs, metrics and p95 or p99 latency to confirm scope and when it started | Use tracing or APM to break the time down into DB queries, external calls and CPU | Check slow queries with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and look for N+1 queries or missing indexes | Profile the code with a tool like py-spy and check for blocking calls in async code | Correlate with recent deploys or data growth, fix, and verify with the same metrics

text: How does FastAPI internally handle an endpoint defined with def versus async def, and what are the performance implications under heavy load?
ideal_key_points: async def endpoints run directly on the event loop | Plain def endpoints run in a threadpool managed by AnyIO, which defaults to about 40 threads | Blocking code inside async def stalls every request on that worker | Under heavy load the threadpool can be exhausted, causing queuing even though CPU is idle | Throughput is scaled with multiple worker processes behind Uvicorn or Gunicorn, since one process is limited by the GIL

text: Explain the difference between an INNER JOIN, a LEFT JOIN and a FULL OUTER JOIN.
ideal_key_points: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables | LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where there is no match on the right | FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, with NULLs where either side has no match | The join condition is specified in the ON clause

text: What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key?
ideal_key_points: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL | A table has only one primary key, which may be composite | A foreign key references the primary key or a unique key of another table | Foreign keys enforce referential integrity | ON DELETE options like CASCADE or RESTRICT control what happens to child rows

text: What does ACID stand for in databases?
ideal_key_points: Atomicity means a transaction is all or nothing | Consistency means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints | Isolation means concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other | Durability means committed data survives crashes, typically via a write-ahead log

text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
ideal_key_points: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping | HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation | Aggregate functions like COUNT or SUM cannot be used in WHERE | Filtering in WHERE when possible is more efficient because fewer rows are aggregated

text: What is a database index, how does it speed up queries, and what does it cost?
ideal_key_points: An index is a separate data structure, usually a B-tree, that maps column values to rows | It turns full table scans into logarithmic lookups for filters, joins and sorts | Every insert, update and delete must also update the index, slowing writes | Indexes consume storage and memory | Columns with low selectivity often do not benefit from an index

text: What is the N plus 1 query problem and how do you fix it?
ideal_key_points: One query loads a list of parent rows, then one extra query runs per row to load related data | It usually comes from ORM lazy loading inside a loop | Fix it with a join or eager loading, such as joinedload or selectinload in SQLAlchemy | Detect it by logging SQL queries or counting queries per request in tests

text: What is database normalization, and when might you deliberately denormalize?
ideal_key_points: Normalization organizes tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies | First normal form requires atomic values with no repeating groups | Second normal form removes partial dependencies on a composite key, and third normal form removes transitive dependencies | Denormalization duplicates data to make reads faster or avoid expensive joins | Denormalizing adds the cost of keeping copies consistent

text: What are the pros and cons of using an ORM like SQLAlchemy compared to writing raw SQL?
ideal_key_points: An ORM maps tables to classes and boosts productivity and readability | It parameterizes queries, protecting against SQL injection | It can hide inefficient queries and cause problems like N plus 1 | Complex queries may be harder to express or optimize, so raw SQL is an escape hatch | SQLAlchemy uses a session as a unit of work that tracks changes and commits them together

text: What are database migrations, and why use a tool like Alembic instead of changing the schema by hand?
ideal_key_points: Migrations are versioned, ordered scripts that change the schema | They keep schema changes in version control alongside code | Every environment can be brought to the same schema reproducibly | Alembic supports upgrade and downgrade and can autogenerate migrations from models, which must be reviewed | Migrations are typically run as a step in the deployment pipeline

text: When would you store data in a PostgreSQL JSONB column instead of regular columns?
ideal_key_points: JSONB stores JSON in a decomposed binary format that supports indexing, unlike plain JSON | It suits semi-structured or variable data such as metadata or LLM tool outputs | It can be queried with operators like arrow, double arrow and containment, and indexed with GIN | You lose column-level types, constraints and some query planner statistics | Fields that are queried or joined frequently should be regular columns

text: How would you use EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE to investigate a slow query?
ideal_key_points: EXPLAIN shows the planned execution without running the query | EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports real timings and row counts | Look for sequential scans on large tables where an index scan is expected | Compare estimated rows with actual rows, since big gaps suggest stale statistics that ANALYZE can refresh | Fix by adding the right index, rewriting the query or reducing the rows fetched

text: How does the column order in a composite index matter? Give an example.
ideal_key_points: A composite index can be used for queries that filter on a leftmost prefix of its columns | An index on user_id then created_at helps queries by user_id alone but not by created_at alone | Put equality-filtered columns before range-filtered or sorted columns | A covering index or INCLUDE columns allows index-only scans | Wrapping a column in a function prevents index use unless there is an expression index

text: Explain transaction isolation levels and the anomalies each one prevents.
ideal_key_points: Anomalies include dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads and lost updates | Read uncommitted allows dirty reads, read committed prevents them | Repeatable read prevents non-repeatable reads and serializable prevents all anomalies | PostgreSQL defaults to read committed and uses MVCC so readers do not block writers | Serializable can fail with serialization errors that the application must retry, and SELECT FOR UPDATE is another way to prevent lost updates

text: How would you implement vector similarity search inside PostgreSQL for a RAG application, and what trade-offs would you consider?
ideal_key_points: Use the pgvector extension and store embeddings in a vector column | Query with distance operators for cosine or L2 distance, ordering by distance with a LIMIT | Add an approximate nearest neighbour index such as HNSW or IVFFlat, trading recall for speed | Combining similarity with SQL metadata filters and joins is a key advantage | A dedicated vector database may scale better for very large collections or heavy query loads

text: How would you add a NOT NULL column to a table with 100 million rows in production without downtime?
ideal_key_points: Use an expand and contract approach instead of a single blocking change | First add the column as nullable, or with a constant default, which recent PostgreSQL versions apply as a fast metadata-only change | Backfill existing rows in small batches to avoid long locks and replication lag | Then add the NOT NULL constraint, for example via a CHECK constraint created NOT VALID and validated separately | Deploy application code that works with both schemas, set lock_timeout, and build any indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY

text: What is Redis, and what are some common use cases for it in a backend?
ideal_key_points: Redis is an in-memory key-value data store, which makes it very fast | It is used for caching, session storage and rate limiting counters | It supports data structures such as strings, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets | It also offers pub/sub and streams for messaging | It can persist data with RDB snapshots or an append-only file

text: Why would you introduce a message queue between two services?
ideal_key_points: It decouples producers from consumers so they can evolve and fail independently | Work can be processed asynchronously so the API responds quickly | It absorbs traffic spikes by buffering messages | Consumers can be scaled independently and failed messages retried

text: Explain the cache-aside pattern and how it differs from write-through caching.
ideal_key_points: In cache-aside the application reads the cache first and on a miss reads the database and populates the cache | On writes, cache-aside updates the database and invalidates the cache entry | Write-through writes to the cache and the database together on every write | Write-through keeps the cache fresh but adds write latency and caches data that may never be read | A TTL is usually set as a safety net against stale entries

text: How does Celery work, and what are its main components?
ideal_key_points: The application sends tasks to a broker such as RabbitMQ or Redis | Worker processes consume tasks from the broker and execute them | An optional result backend stores task results and states | It supports retries, rate limits and periodic tasks via Celery beat | Task arguments must be serializable and tasks should be idempotent because they may run more than once

text: How do you handle failures in a message consumer? Explain retries, exponential backoff and dead-letter queues.
ideal_key_points: Retry transient failures like timeouts, but not permanent ones like validation errors | Use exponential backoff with jitter to avoid hammering a struggling dependency | Cap the number of retries | After the maximum, move the message to a dead-letter queue instead of blocking the queue | Monitor and alert on the DLQ, inspect and replay messages, and make consumers idempotent

text: What strategies do you know for cache invalidation, and what problems can occur?
ideal_key_points: Time-based expiry with a TTL bounds staleness | Explicitly delete the cache key when the underlying data changes, which is safer than updating it | Versioned or namespaced keys allow invalidating many entries at once | Races between a write and a concurrent cache refill can leave stale data cached | Event-driven invalidation, for example via change events, helps across services

text: How would you cache LLM responses in a GenAI application? Compare exact-match and semantic caching.
ideal_key_points: Exact-match caching keys on a hash of the prompt, model and generation parameters | It is only safe when outputs are expected to be deterministic or reuse is acceptable | Semantic caching embeds the query and returns a cached answer for sufficiently similar queries above a threshold | Semantic caching can return wrong answers on false matches, so the threshold must be tuned | Invalidate when the model, prompt template or underlying data changes, and never share user-specific responses across users

text: Compare RabbitMQ and Kafka. When would you pick one over the other?
ideal_key_points: RabbitMQ is a message broker with flexible routing via exchanges, and messages are removed once acknowledged | Kafka is a distributed append-only log where messages are retained and can be replayed | Kafka scales through partitions and consumer groups that track offsets | Kafka guarantees ordering only within a partition | RabbitMQ suits task queues and RPC-style work, while Kafka suits high-throughput event streaming and analytics

text: What is a cache stampede, and how would you prevent it?
ideal_key_points: A stampede happens when a popular key expires and many requests miss at once and hit the database together | Use a lock or single-flight so only one request recomputes the value, for example with Redis SET NX | Serve the stale value while one request refreshes it in the background | Add random jitter to TTLs so many keys do not expire at the same time | Probabilistic early expiration refreshes hot keys before they expire

text: Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once message delivery. How do you achieve effectively exactly-once processing in practice?
ideal_key_points: At-most-once acknowledges before processing and may lose messages | At-least-once acknowledges after processing and may deliver duplicates | True exactly-once delivery across systems is impractical, so aim for at-least-once plus idempotent processing | Deduplicate with a unique message ID stored in the same transaction as the side effect | The transactional outbox pattern publishes events reliably alongside DB writes, and Kafka offers transactions for exactly-once within Kafka

text: What is the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
ideal_key_points: An image is a read-only template made of layers containing the app and its dependencies | A container is a running instance of an image | A container adds a thin writable layer on top of the image | Many containers can run from the same image | Images are built from a Dockerfile and stored in a registry

text: What is Docker Compose used for?
ideal_key_points: It defines and runs multi-container applications from a YAML file | Each service declares its image or build, ports, environment variables and volumes | Services on the same network reach each other by service name | It is mainly used for local development and testing, for example an API plus Postgres plus Redis | depends_on alone does not wait for readiness unless combined with a healthcheck condition

text: How does Docker layer caching work, and how should you order instructions in a Dockerfile for a Python app?
ideal_key_points: Each instruction such as RUN or COPY creates a layer | A layer is reused from cache if the instruction and its inputs are unchanged | Once a layer changes, all following layers are rebuilt | Copy requirements.txt and install dependencies before copying the application code | Then code changes do not trigger a slow reinstall of dependencies

text: What is a multi-stage Docker build and why is it useful?
ideal_key_points: A Dockerfile can contain multiple FROM stages | Build tools and compilers are used in an early builder stage | Only the needed artifacts, such as wheels or a virtual environment, are copied into a slim final stage | The final image is smaller and has a reduced attack surface | Build secrets and tooling do not end up in the runtime image

text: What is the difference between Docker volumes and bind mounts, and how do you persist data from a container?
ideal_key_points: A container's writable layer is lost when the container is removed | Volumes are managed by Docker and are the preferred way to persist data like database files | Bind mounts map a specific host path into the container | Bind mounts are handy in development for live code reloading | Volumes are more portable and do not depend on the host directory structure

text: How should you manage configuration and secrets like API keys for a backend application?
ideal_key_points: Keep config in environment variables, following the twelve-factor approach | Load and validate settings with something like pydantic-settings | Never commit secrets to git, and keep .env files in .gitignore | Do not bake secrets into Docker images, since ARG and ENV values are visible in image history | Use a secret manager like AWS Secrets Manager, Vault or Kubernetes secrets, and rotate keys

text: Explain the basic Kubernetes objects: Pod, Deployment and Service.
ideal_key_points: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit, running one or more containers that share network and storage | A Deployment manages a set of identical Pod replicas and performs rolling updates | A Service gives Pods a stable DNS name and IP and load-balances across them | Liveness and readiness probes tell Kubernetes when to restart a Pod or send it traffic

text: Describe a CI/CD pipeline you would set up for a FastAPI service.
ideal_key_points: On every pull request, run linting, type checking and tests | Build a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA and push it to a registry | Deploy automatically to staging, run database migrations and smoke tests | Promote to production with a manual approval or automated checks | Keep secrets in the CI secret store and have a clear rollback strategy

text: A container works on your laptop but crashes or misbehaves in production. How would you debug it?
ideal_key_points: Check container logs and the exit code, for example 137 usually means killed for out of memory | Compare environment variables, secrets and config between environments | Check networking, such as binding to 0.0.0.0 instead of localhost and using correct service hostnames | Check CPU architecture mismatches like arm64 versus amd64 images | Check resource limits, file permissions and failing health checks

text: Your Docker image for a PyTorch inference service is 8 gigabytes. How would you reduce it?
ideal_key_points: Use a slim Python base image and avoid unnecessary system packages | Install the CPU-only PyTorch wheel if a GPU is not needed, since CUDA libraries are huge | Use a multi-stage build and pip install with no cache | Add a .dockerignore to exclude data, notebooks and git history | Consider downloading model weights at startup or from a mounted volume instead of baking them in, trading off startup time

text: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments.
ideal_key_points: Rolling deployments replace instances gradually with no extra environment | Blue-green runs two full environments and switches traffic at once, allowing instant rollback but doubling resources | Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version and increases it while monitoring metrics | Canary limits the blast radius of a bad release | All strategies need backward-compatible database schema changes because old and new versions run together

text: What is the difference between unit tests, integration tests and end-to-end tests?
ideal_key_points: Unit tests check a single function or class in isolation, are fast and mock dependencies | Integration tests check that components work together, such as the API with a real database | End-to-end tests exercise the whole system as a user would | Moving up the levels, tests become slower, more realistic and more brittle

text: What is test-driven development?
ideal_key_points: Write a failing test before writing the code | Write the minimum code to make the test pass | Refactor while keeping the tests green, the red-green-refactor cycle | It encourages small, testable designs and gives a safety net for changes

text: What are pytest fixtures, and how do fixture scopes work?
ideal_key_points: Fixtures are functions decorated with pytest.fixture that provide setup data or resources | Tests request a fixture simply by naming it as a parameter | Scopes include function, class, module and session, controlling how often a fixture is created | Using yield lets a fixture run teardown code after the test | Shared fixtures live in conftest.py

text: What is mocking in tests, and what are common pitfalls?
ideal_key_points: Mocking replaces a real dependency with a fake object to isolate the code under test | unittest.mock provides patch, Mock, MagicMock and AsyncMock | You must patch the name where it is looked up, not where it is defined | Assertions like assert_called_once_with verify interactions | Over-mocking couples tests to implementation details and can hide real integration bugs

text: Is 100 percent code coverage a good goal? Explain your view using the testing pyramid.
ideal_key_points: The pyramid suggests many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few end-to-end tests | Coverage only shows which lines ran, not that behaviour was correctly asserted | Branch coverage is more meaningful than line coverage | Chasing 100 percent leads to low-value tests, so focus on critical paths and edge cases | Mutation testing can measure how good the tests really are

text: How would you test a FastAPI endpoint that depends on a database and an authenticated user?
ideal_key_points: Use FastAPI's TestClient or httpx AsyncClient to call the app in-process | Use app.dependency_overrides to replace the DB session and current-user dependencies | Run against a dedicated test database, ideally the same engine as production, for example via testcontainers | Isolate tests by wrapping each in a transaction that is rolled back, or by resetting data | Assert on status codes, response bodies and resulting DB state

text: How would you write tests for code that calls an external LLM API?
ideal_key_points: Mock the LLM client in unit tests so tests are fast, free and deterministic | Use recorded responses or fixtures to test parsing of real response formats | Simulate failures like timeouts, 429s and malformed output to test retries and error handling | Assert on structure and properties of outputs rather than exact text | Keep separate evaluation suites to measure output quality against real models

text: Some of your tests pass locally but fail randomly in CI. What causes flaky tests and how would you fix them?
ideal_key_points: Timing issues such as fixed sleeps and race conditions in async code | Shared state or test order dependence, which tools like pytest-randomly can expose | Dependence on external networks or services | Uncontrolled randomness or current time, fixed by seeding and freezing time | Reproduce by rerunning, quarantine if needed, but fix the root cause instead of adding retries

text: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
ideal_key_points: Authentication verifies who the user is, for example with a password or token | Authorization decides what an authenticated user is allowed to do | Authentication happens first, then authorization | Failing authentication maps to 401 and failing authorization maps to 403 | Role-based access control is a common authorization model

text: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
ideal_key_points: Untrusted input concatenated into a SQL string can change the query's meaning | It can leak, modify or delete data and bypass login checks | Use parameterized queries or prepared statements so input is always treated as data | ORMs parameterize queries by default, but raw SQL with string formatting is still dangerous | Give the database user least privilege

text: How should user passwords be stored in a database?
ideal_key_points: Never store plaintext or reversibly encrypted passwords | Use a slow, salted password hashing algorithm such as Argon2, bcrypt or scrypt | Each password gets a unique random salt, which defeats rainbow tables | Fast hashes like MD5 or plain SHA-256 are unsuitable because they are easy to brute force | Verify by hashing the input with the stored salt and increase the cost factor over time

text: What is CORS and why do browsers enforce it?
ideal_key_points: Browsers enforce a same-origin policy that blocks scripts from reading responses from other origins | CORS lets a server allow specific origins via headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin | Non-simple requests trigger a preflight OPTIONS request | CORS is enforced by browsers, not servers, so it does not protect an API from curl or scripts | A wildcard origin cannot be combined with credentials, so list allowed origins explicitly

text: What does HTTPS provide, and roughly how does TLS work?
ideal_key_points: It provides encryption, integrity and server authentication | The server presents a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority | The handshake uses asymmetric cryptography to agree on a shared key | Bulk data is then encrypted with fast symmetric encryption | HSTS tells browsers to always use HTTPS for the site

text: Compare JWT-based authentication with server-side sessions.
ideal_key_points: Sessions store state on the server and give the client a session ID cookie, making revocation easy | JWTs are signed, self-contained tokens with a header, payload and signature, verified without a DB lookup | JWT payloads are base64 encoded, not encrypted, so they must not contain secrets | Revoking JWTs is hard, so use short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens or a denylist | Tokens in localStorage are exposed to XSS, while httpOnly cookies avoid that but need CSRF protection

text: Explain common rate limiting algorithms and how you would implement rate limiting for an API.
ideal_key_points: Token bucket refills tokens at a fixed rate and allows short bursts | Leaky bucket processes requests at a constant rate, smoothing bursts | Fixed window counters are simple but allow bursts at window boundaries | Sliding window log or counter is more accurate | Store counters in Redis, for example INCR with EXPIRE, and return 429 with a Retry-After header

text: What are XSS and CSRF attacks, and how do you defend against each?
ideal_key_points: XSS injects malicious scripts that run in other users' browsers | Defend against XSS by escaping output, sanitizing HTML and using a Content Security Policy | CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request carrying their cookies | Defend against CSRF with SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens | Tokens sent in an Authorization header are not exposed to CSRF but are exposed to XSS if stored in JavaScript-accessible storage

text: Walk me through the OAuth 2 authorization code flow, for example Sign in with Google.
ideal_key_points: The roles are the resource owner, client app, authorization server and resource server | The app redirects the user to the authorization server, where they log in and consent | The authorization server redirects back with a short-lived authorization code | The backend exchanges the code plus client credentials for an access token, and PKCE protects public clients | OAuth 2 is for authorization, while OpenID Connect adds an ID token for authentication

text: Your backend lets users chat with an LLM that can call internal tools. How do you defend against prompt injection?
ideal_key_points: Prompt injection is when untrusted input, directly or via retrieved documents, overrides the model's instructions | It cannot be fully prevented by prompt wording alone | Treat LLM output as untrusted and validate tool calls and arguments before executing | Give tools least privilege and require human confirmation for sensitive actions | Never put secrets in prompts, enforce authorization outside the model, and add input and output filtering

text: Compare the HS256 and RS256 algorithms for signing JWTs, and what attacks should your token validation guard against?
ideal_key_points: HS256 uses one shared secret both to sign and verify, so every verifier can also mint tokens | RS256 signs with a private key and verifies with a public key, often published via a JWKS endpoint | Pin the allowed algorithms to prevent alg none and algorithm-confusion attacks | Always validate exp, iss and aud claims | Use a kid header to support key rotation

text: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
ideal_key_points: Vertical scaling means adding more CPU, RAM or disk to a single machine | Horizontal scaling means adding more machines or instances | Vertical scaling is simpler but has hardware limits and a single point of failure | Horizontal scaling needs stateless services and a load balancer

text: What does a load balancer do, and what algorithms can it use?
