ideal_key_points: It distributes incoming traffic across multiple server instances | It improves availability by removing unhealthy instances using health checks | Common algorithms are round robin, least connections and IP hash | It may operate at layer 4 on TCP or layer 7 on HTTP | Sticky sessions are possible but stateless services are preferred

text: Design a simple Pastebin service where users can paste text and share a link.
ideal_key_points: API to create a paste returning a unique ID, and to fetch by ID | Generate short unique IDs, for example random base62 strings with a collision check | Store metadata in a database and large content in object storage like S3 | Support expiry with a TTL and a cleanup job | Cache popular pastes and rate limit creation to prevent abuse

text: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly.
ideal_key_points: Endpoints to create a short code and to redirect from the code to the long URL | Generate codes via base62 encoding of an auto-increment ID or random strings with collision checks | Redirect with 301 or 302, where 302 allows click analytics | The system is read-heavy, so cache hot mappings in Redis in front of the database | Handle custom aliases, expiry and abuse prevention with rate limiting

text: Explain the CAP theorem and how it influences design choices.
ideal_key_points: CAP covers consistency, availability and partition tolerance | During a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability | Partition tolerance is not optional in real distributed systems | CP systems reject some requests to stay consistent, AP systems serve possibly stale data | Many systems offer tunable or eventual consistency depending on the use case

text: Design a system where users upload resume PDFs that are then parsed and analysed by an LLM.
ideal_key_points: Upload directly to object storage with a presigned URL to keep large files off the API servers | Validate file type and size and scan for malware | Record a job in the database and enqueue it to a task queue | Workers extract text, call the LLM, and store results, with retries and a dead-letter queue | The client tracks progress by polling a status endpoint or via SSE or webhooks

text: Design the backend for a chatbot that streams responses and remembers conversation history.
ideal_key_points: Store conversations and messages in a database keyed by user and conversation ID | Build the prompt from a window of recent messages plus a summary of older ones to fit the context limit | Stream tokens to the client with SSE and persist the full message once complete | Handle client disconnects, timeouts and LLM provider errors gracefully | Add authentication, per-user rate limits and token usage tracking

text: Design an API for long-running tasks like video transcription, where processing can take several minutes.
ideal_key_points: The submit endpoint returns 202 Accepted with a job ID immediately | Jobs are pushed to a queue and processed by a separate pool of workers | A status endpoint reports states such as queued, running, succeeded and failed | Clients can poll, or receive a webhook or SSE notification on completion | Make jobs idempotent with retries, timeouts and a dead-letter queue, and store results in object storage

text: Design a distributed rate limiter for a public API running on many servers.
ideal_key_points: Limits are keyed per API key, user or IP and may differ by plan tier | Use a shared store like Redis so all servers see the same counters | Implement token bucket or sliding window with atomic operations, such as a Lua script | Return 429 with Retry-After and rate limit headers | Decide fail-open versus fail-closed if Redis is down, and consider local limits to reduce latency

text: Design a notification service that sends emails, SMS and push notifications.
ideal_key_points: Producers publish notification events to a queue rather than calling providers directly | Separate workers per channel call providers such as an email or SMS gateway | Respect user preferences, opt-outs, templates and quiet hours | Retry with backoff, deduplicate with idempotency keys and use a dead-letter queue | Rate limit per user and provider, and track delivery status for observability

text: Design an LLM gateway that routes requests across multiple model providers with fallback and cost tracking.
ideal_key_points: A single internal API abstracts provider-specific request and response formats | Route by model, cost or latency, and fall back to another provider on errors or timeouts | Enforce per-team rate limits and budgets using token counts | Log tokens, latency and cost per request for usage dashboards and billing | Add response caching, retries with backoff, secret management for provider keys and PII redaction

text: Design a webhook delivery system that reliably notifies customer endpoints when events happen.
ideal_key_points: Persist events and enqueue delivery jobs instead of sending inline | Retry failed deliveries with exponential backoff over hours, then mark as failed or send to a DLQ | Sign payloads with HMAC so receivers can verify authenticity | Include an event ID so receivers can deduplicate, since delivery is at-least-once | Isolate slow customer endpoints with per-endpoint queues and timeouts, and provide delivery logs and replay

text: Design the backend for a document question-answering system using retrieval-augmented generation for thousands of companies.
ideal_key_points: An ingestion pipeline parses documents, chunks them, embeds the chunks and stores them in a vector index asynchronously | Enforce strict tenant isolation, filtering retrieval by tenant ID or using separate indexes | At query time embed the question, retrieve top chunks, optionally rerank, and generate with citations | Handle document updates and deletions by re-indexing and removing stale vectors | Control cost and latency with caching, streaming responses, and monitoring retrieval quality with evaluations

text: Design a real-time chat application like WhatsApp Web using WebSockets.
ideal_key_points: Clients hold persistent WebSocket connections to gateway servers | Track which server each user is connected to in a shared store like Redis | Route messages between servers via pub/sub or a message broker | Persist messages before acknowledging, with message IDs for ordering and deduplication | Deliver offline messages on reconnect, handle presence and typing indicators, and scale stateful connections with sticky load balancing

text: Design a distributed job queue system from scratch, similar to Celery or Sidekiq.
ideal_key_points: Producers enqueue jobs with a payload, priority and options into durable storage | Workers lease jobs with a visibility timeout so crashed workers' jobs become available again | Workers acknowledge on completion, giving at-least-once delivery that requires idempotent jobs | Support retries with backoff, dead-letter queues, scheduled jobs and priorities | Provide monitoring of queue depth, latency and failures, and scale workers based on queue depth

text: Design a system to serve a machine learning model behind an API that can autoscale with traffic.
ideal_key_points: Package the model in a container behind a stateless API, loading the model once at startup | Run replicas behind a load balancer with readiness probes that pass only after the model loads | Autoscale on metrics like request rate, latency, GPU utilization or queue depth, not just CPU | Use dynamic batching and consider a dedicated inference server to improve throughput | Handle cold starts, version models with canary rollouts, and monitor latency and prediction drift

text: Design a search autocomplete service that returns suggestions within 50 milliseconds as the user types.
ideal_key_points: Use a prefix structure like a trie or an index of precomputed top suggestions per prefix | Rank suggestions by popularity or recency, recomputed periodically by an offline pipeline | Serve from memory or Redis and cache popular prefixes, including at the edge | Debounce on the client and cap the number of results to reduce load | Shard by prefix for scale and filter offensive or personalized suggestions appropriately

text: What is the difference between the mean, median and mode, and when would you prefer the median over the mean?
ideal_key_points: Mean is the arithmetic average, median is the middle value when sorted, mode is the most frequent value | Mean is sensitive to outliers and skew while the median is robust | Prefer the median for skewed data such as income, house prices or session length | Mode is useful for categorical data | In a right-skewed distribution the mean is typically greater than the median

text: Explain the difference between a population and a sample, and between a parameter and a statistic.
ideal_key_points: Population is the full group of interest, sample is a subset actually observed | Parameter describes the population, such as the true mean, and is usually unknown | Statistic is computed from the sample, such as the sample mean, and estimates the parameter | Random sampling is needed so the sample is representative and statistics are unbiased | Statistics vary from sample to sample, which is described by the sampling distribution

text: What is the normal distribution, and what does the 68-95-99.7 rule tell you?
ideal_key_points: Symmetric bell-shaped continuous distribution defined by mean and standard deviation | Mean, median and mode are equal | About 68 percent of values lie within 1 standard deviation, 95 percent within 2, and 99.7 percent within 3 | Z-score standardizes a value as distance from the mean in standard deviations | Many natural measurements and sampling distributions of means are approximately normal

text: When would you model a variable with a binomial distribution versus a Poisson distribution? Give an example of each.
ideal_key_points: Binomial counts successes in a fixed number n of independent trials with the same success probability p, for example conversions out of 1000 visitors | Binomial mean is n times p and variance is n times p times (1 minus p) | Poisson counts events in a fixed interval of time or space at a constant average rate lambda, for example support tickets per hour | Poisson mean and variance both equal lambda | Binomial approaches Poisson when n is large and p is small with n times p equal to lambda

text: Explain the central limit theorem and why it matters in practice.
ideal_key_points: The distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows, regardless of the population's shape | Requires independent samples and finite variance | Standard error of the mean equals sigma divided by the square root of n | Justifies z-tests, t-tests and confidence intervals on means, such as in A/B tests | Rule of thumb n around 30 or more, but heavily skewed data needs larger samples

text: What is a p-value, and what are the common ways people misinterpret it?
ideal_key_points: Probability of observing data at least as extreme as what was observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true | It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true | It does not measure effect size or practical importance | A large p-value does not prove the null, it only fails to reject it | P-values are affected by sample size and inflated false positives arise from multiple testing or p-hacking

text: How do you interpret a 95 percent confidence interval, and what makes it wider or narrower?
ideal_key_points: If the procedure were repeated many times, about 95 percent of the intervals would contain the true parameter | It is not a 95 percent probability that this specific interval contains the parameter, in the frequentist view | Width depends on the standard error, which shrinks with larger sample size and lower variability | Higher confidence level such as 99 percent produces a wider interval | An interval excluding the null value corresponds to significance at the matching alpha

text: Explain Type one and Type two errors, and how they relate to the significance level and power of a test.
ideal_key_points: Type one error is a false positive, rejecting a true null hypothesis, with probability alpha | Type two error is a false negative, failing to reject a false null, with probability beta | Power equals 1 minus beta, the probability of detecting a true effect | Lowering alpha reduces false positives but increases beta unless sample size increases | Power increases with larger sample size, larger effect size and lower variance

text: A disease affects 1 percent of people, and a test has 99 percent sensitivity and a 5 percent false positive rate. If someone tests positive, walk me through how you would estimate the probability they actually have the disease.
ideal_key_points: Apply Bayes' theorem: P(disease given positive) equals P(positive given disease) times P(disease) divided by P(positive) | P(positive) equals 0.99 times 0.01 plus 0.05 times 0.99, which is about 0.0594 | Posterior is about 0.0099 divided by 0.0594, roughly 17 percent | Low base rate means most positives are false positives, the base rate fallacy | A second independent positive test would raise the probability substantially

text: You notice that users who use a particular feature have much higher retention. How would you figure out whether the feature actually causes better retention?
ideal_key_points: Correlation does not imply causation | Confounders such as user engagement level may drive both feature use and retention, which is selection bias | Reverse causality is possible, retained users have more time to discover the feature | Gold standard is a randomized experiment, such as randomly exposing or promoting the feature | If no experiment is possible use quasi-experimental methods like matching, difference-in-differences or instrumental variables

text: What is Simpson's paradox? Give an example and explain how you would guard against it.
ideal_key_points: A trend present within every subgroup reverses or disappears when the groups are combined | Caused by a confounding variable that is unevenly distributed across groups, such as group sizes differing | Example: a treatment has a higher success rate in both mild and severe cases but a lower overall rate because it was given mostly to severe cases | Guard against it by segmenting by likely confounders and using stratified analysis | Randomization balances confounders so aggregate comparisons are valid

text: Compare Pearson and Spearman correlation. When would you use each?
ideal_key_points: Pearson measures the strength of a linear relationship between two continuous variables | Spearman is Pearson correlation computed on ranks and measures monotonic relationships | Spearman is more robust to outliers and works with ordinal data | Both range from minus 1 to 1 and zero correlation does not imply independence | A strong nonlinear but monotonic relationship gives high Spearman but lower Pearson

text: Explain maximum likelihood estimation. How would you estimate the rate parameter of a Poisson distribution from observed counts?
ideal_key_points: MLE chooses parameter values that maximize the probability (likelihood) of the observed data | In practice maximize the log-likelihood because products become sums | Take the derivative of the log-likelihood, set it to zero and solve | For Poisson the MLE of lambda is the sample mean of the counts | MLE is consistent and asymptotically efficient but can overfit with small samples

text: Compare the frequentist and Bayesian approaches to statistical inference.
ideal_key_points: Frequentists treat parameters as fixed unknowns and probability as long-run frequency | Bayesians treat parameters as random variables with a prior distribution | Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior | Bayesian credible intervals give a direct probability statement about the parameter, unlike confidence intervals | Priors allow incorporating domain knowledge but add subjectivity, and the prior's influence shrinks as data grows

text: You flip a fair coin until you get two heads in a row. Walk me through how you would compute the expected number of flips.
ideal_key_points: Define states by progress: E0 with no trailing head and E1 with one trailing head | E0 equals 1 plus half of E1 plus half of E0 | E1 equals 1 plus half of zero plus half of E0, since a tail resets progress | Solving the equations gives E0 equal to 6 flips | Approach generalizes to Markov chain or first-step analysis, and n heads in a row gives 2 to the power n plus 1 minus 2

text: Revenue per user is very heavy-tailed, with a few whales. Why does that break standard inference on the average, and how would you handle it?
ideal_key_points: Extreme values dominate the sample mean, making it unstable with a very large variance | CLT convergence is slow, so normal approximations and t-tests may be unreliable at practical sample sizes | Use bootstrap confidence intervals instead of normal-based intervals | Consider winsorizing or capping outliers, log transforms, or analyzing medians and quantiles | Alternatively split into conversion rate and revenue among payers, and use larger samples or variance reduction

text: What is an A/B test, and why do we randomly assign users to the groups?
ideal_key_points: A controlled experiment comparing a control version A and a treatment version B on a chosen metric | Random assignment balances both observed and unobserved confounders between groups | Allows the difference in outcomes to be attributed causally to the change | Groups should run simultaneously to avoid time-based biases | Result is analyzed with a statistical test to see if the difference exceeds chance

text: In an A/B test, what are the null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis?
ideal_key_points: Null hypothesis states there is no difference between control and treatment on the metric | Alternative states there is a difference, either two-sided or in a specific direction | We collect data and test whether evidence is strong enough to reject the null at significance level alpha | Failing to reject the null does not prove there is no effect | Hypotheses and the metric should be defined before the test starts

text: What are primary metrics and guardrail metrics in an experiment? Give an example of each.
ideal_key_points: Primary or success metric is the one the decision is based on, such as checkout conversion rate | Guardrail metrics must not get worse, such as page load time, error rate, or unsubscribe rate | Primary metric should be chosen before the test to avoid cherry-picking | Guardrails protect user experience and business health from unintended harm | Secondary metrics help explain the mechanism but are not the decision criterion

text: Walk me through how you would design an A/B test for a new checkout button on an e-commerce site.
ideal_key_points: State a clear hypothesis and pick a primary metric such as checkout conversion plus guardrails | Choose the randomization unit, usually user, and split traffic randomly | Compute sample size from baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, alpha and power | Run for a fixed duration covering full weekly cycles without stopping early | Check sample ratio mismatch, then analyze with an appropriate test and confidence interval before deciding

text: What factors determine the sample size you need for an A/B test?
ideal_key_points: Baseline metric value and its variance | Minimum detectable effect, where sample size scales with one over the effect size squared | Significance level alpha, commonly 0.05 | Desired power, commonly 80 percent | Number of variants and traffic allocation split, plus whether the test is one-sided or two-sided

text: What is statistical power, and why is running an underpowered experiment a problem?
ideal_key_points: Power is the probability of detecting a true effect of a given size, equal to 1 minus beta | Commonly targeted at 80 percent | Underpowered tests often miss real effects, leading to false negatives | Significant results from underpowered tests tend to overestimate the effect size, the winner's curse | Fix by increasing sample size or duration, reducing variance, or targeting a larger effect

text: Why is it a problem to check A/B test results every day and stop as soon as the result is significant?
ideal_key_points: Repeated peeking with a fixed alpha inflates the false positive rate well above 5 percent | P-values fluctuate and will likely cross the threshold by chance at some point | Decide the sample size or duration in advance and analyze once | If early stopping is needed use sequential testing methods such as alpha spending or always-valid p-values | Stopping early also misses weekly seasonality and novelty effects

text: What is the novelty effect in A/B testing, and how would you detect and handle it?
ideal_key_points: Users react to something new simply because it is new, causing a temporary lift that fades | The opposite, change aversion or primacy effect, causes a temporary dip | Detect by plotting the treatment effect over time and seeing it decay or grow | Compare new users versus existing users, since new users have no prior expectation | Run the test longer or use holdout groups to measure the long-term effect

text: If you test 20 different metrics in an experiment at a 0.05 significance level, what problem arises and how would you handle it?
ideal_key_points: Multiple comparisons problem: chance of at least one false positive is about 1 minus 0.95 to the power 20, roughly 64 percent | Bonferroni correction tests each at alpha divided by number of tests, which is conservative | Holm method is a less conservative step-down alternative controlling family-wise error | Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate and is more powerful | Pre-register one primary metric and treat others as exploratory

text: What is a sample ratio mismatch, and why should you check for it before analyzing an experiment?
ideal_key_points: SRM is when the observed split of users between groups differs significantly from the intended split, such as 50.5 to 49.5 on large traffic | Detected with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test on group counts | Indicates a bug in randomization, logging, redirects, or bots being filtered unevenly | Results of a test with SRM are untrustworthy because groups may no longer be comparable | Investigate and fix the root cause rather than analyzing the biased data

text: How would you choose the randomization unit for an experiment, such as user, session, or page view?
ideal_key_points: User-level randomization gives a consistent experience and avoids users seeing both variants | Session or page-view randomization gives more units and power but risks contamination and inconsistent experience | Randomization unit should be at least as coarse as the unit where effects can spill over | If the analysis unit differs from the randomization unit, observations are correlated and variance must be computed with the delta method or bootstrap at the randomization unit | Logged-out users may need cookie or device-level randomization

text: Your A/B test shows a statistically significant 0.1 percent lift in conversion. How would you decide whether to launch?
ideal_key_points: Statistical significance is not the same as practical or business significance | Look at the confidence interval and whether even the lower bound justifies the change | Weigh implementation, maintenance and opportunity costs against expected revenue impact | Check guardrail metrics and consistency across key segments and over time | Consider long-term effects, novelty, and whether the minimum detectable effect was set in advance

text: How would you run an experiment on a social network or two-sided marketplace where users influence each other?
ideal_key_points: Network effects or interference violate SUTVA, the assumption that one unit's outcome is unaffected by others' assignment | Interference biases the naive treatment effect estimate, often toward zero or in either direction in marketplaces | Use cluster-based randomization, such as by graph communities or geographic regions | Use switchback experiments that alternate treatment over time windows in a market | Fewer independent clusters means lower power, so variance must be computed at cluster level

text: Explain CUPED or other variance reduction techniques in A/B testing and why they help.
ideal_key_points: CUPED uses a pre-experiment covariate, usually the same metric before the test, that correlates with the outcome | Adjusted metric is Y minus theta times the covariate deviation from its mean, with theta equal to covariance over variance of the covariate | Variance is reduced by a factor of 1 minus the squared correlation, without biasing the treatment effect | Lower variance means smaller sample size or shorter tests for the same power | Other methods include stratification, regression adjustment, and capping outliers

text: When you cannot run a randomized experiment, what methods would you use to estimate the causal effect of a product launch?
ideal_key_points: Difference-in-differences compares change over time in treated versus untreated groups, assuming parallel trends | Synthetic control builds a weighted combination of untreated units to mimic the treated one | Regression discontinuity exploits a cutoff that determines treatment | Propensity score matching or weighting balances observed confounders only | Interrupted time series models the pre-launch trend, and all methods need assumption checks and placebo tests

text: Your A/B test is randomized by user but the metric is click-through rate computed per page view, and the p-value looks surprisingly tiny. What might be wrong and how would you fix the analysis?
ideal_key_points: Page views from the same user are correlated, so they are not independent observations | Treating page views as independent underestimates the variance and inflates significance | CTR is a ratio metric whose denominator is random at the user level | Use the delta method to compute variance of the ratio at the user level, or bootstrap by resampling users | Alternatively aggregate to per-user metrics, keeping analysis unit consistent with randomization unit

text: What is the difference between COUNT star, COUNT of a column, and COUNT DISTINCT of a column?
ideal_key_points: COUNT star counts all rows including rows with NULLs | COUNT of a column counts only rows where that column is not NULL | COUNT DISTINCT counts unique non-NULL values | COUNT DISTINCT is more expensive because it needs deduplication | Choice matters for metrics, for example counting events versus counting unique users

text: Explain the difference between ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK window functions.
ideal_key_points: All assign numbers within a partition based on an ORDER BY | ROW_NUMBER gives unique sequential numbers even for ties, with arbitrary tie order | RANK gives tied rows the same rank and skips the following ranks, such as 1, 1, 3 | DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps, such as 1, 1, 2 | Choice depends on whether ties should share a position, for example top-N per group

text: How would you find duplicate records in a table, and how would you remove them while keeping one copy of each?
ideal_key_points: Define what makes a duplicate, the set of business key columns | Find duplicates with GROUP BY on the key columns and HAVING count greater than 1 | Use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the key and ordered by a tiebreaker like latest updated timestamp | Keep rows where row number equals 1 and delete or filter out the rest | Alternatively create a new deduplicated table, and prevent recurrence with a unique constraint

text: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL, and which one is faster?
ideal_key_points: Both combine result sets of queries with the same number and compatible types of columns | UNION removes duplicate rows | UNION ALL keeps all rows including duplicates | UNION ALL is faster because it skips the sort or hash step needed for deduplication | Use UNION ALL when the inputs are known to be disjoint or duplicates are wanted

text: Explain the logical order in which the clauses of a SQL query are evaluated.
ideal_key_points: FROM and JOINs first, then WHERE | Then GROUP BY, then HAVING | Then SELECT including window functions, then DISTINCT | Then ORDER BY, then LIMIT or OFFSET | This is why a SELECT alias usually cannot be used in WHERE, and why window functions cannot be filtered in WHERE without a subquery or CTE

text: How do NULL values behave in SQL comparisons, aggregate functions and joins?
ideal_key_points: Comparisons with NULL, even NULL equals NULL, return unknown rather than true, so use IS NULL | Aggregates like SUM, AVG and COUNT of a column ignore NULLs, while COUNT star does not | AVG ignoring NULLs can differ from treating missing as zero | NULL keys do not match each other in joins | NOT IN with a subquery containing a NULL returns no rows, so prefer NOT EXISTS, and COALESCE replaces NULLs

text: Find the second highest salary in each department. Explain your approach.
ideal_key_points: Use DENSE_RANK partitioned by department and ordered by salary descending | Compute it in a CTE or subquery and filter rank equal to 2 in the outer query, since window functions cannot go in WHERE | DENSE_RANK handles ties so duplicated top salaries do not hide the true second highest | Departments with only one distinct salary return no row, or use a left join to show NULL | Alternative is a correlated subquery for the max salary less than the department's max

text: How would you compute a 7-day rolling average of daily revenue in SQL?
ideal_key_points: First aggregate revenue to one row per day | Use AVG over a window ordered by date with ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW | Missing dates break a row-based window, so join to a calendar table and fill zeros | RANGE with an interval frame works on actual date ranges in databases that support it | First six days have partial windows and may need to be flagged or excluded

text: Explain how you would calculate month-over-month revenue growth using SQL.
ideal_key_points: Aggregate revenue by month using a date truncation function | Use LAG over months ordered by month to get the previous month's revenue | Growth equals current minus previous, divided by previous, times 100 | Handle the first month and zero previous revenue to avoid division by zero, for example with NULLIF | Missing months should be filled from a calendar table so LAG compares truly adjacent months

text: How would you find users who made purchases on three or more consecutive days?
ideal_key_points: First reduce to distinct user and purchase date pairs | Assign ROW_NUMBER per user ordered by date | Date minus row number is constant within a run of consecutive days, the gaps-and-islands technique | Group by user and that derived key, and keep groups with count of at least 3 | Alternative uses LAG or LEAD to compare with previous dates, but gaps-and-islands generalizes to any streak length

text: Walk me through writing a cohort retention query: for each signup month, what percentage of users were active in each following month?
ideal_key_points: Assign each user a cohort, the month of their signup or first activity | Join activity events to the cohort and compute months since signup as the month difference | Count distinct active users per cohort and month offset | Divide by the cohort size from the month-zero count, joined or computed with a window function | Result is a cohort by month-offset triangle, and recent cohorts have fewer observable months

text: When would you use a correlated subquery versus a join versus a window function, and what are the performance implications?
ideal_key_points: Correlated subqueries reference the outer row and may run once per row, which can be slow though optimizers sometimes rewrite them | Joins combine tables and are efficient with indexes but can fan out rows with duplicate keys | Window functions compute per-row aggregates without collapsing rows, ideal for ranking, running totals and comparisons to group averages | Window functions often replace a self-join plus group by with a single pass | EXISTS subqueries are good for semi-joins and short-circuit on first match

text: A query joining a large events table to a users table is very slow. How would you diagnose and optimize it?
ideal_key_points: Inspect the execution plan with EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE to find full scans, bad join order or spills | Add or use indexes on join and filter keys, or rely on partitioning and clustering in warehouses for partition pruning | Filter and pre-aggregate early, selecting only needed columns rather than SELECT star | Keep predicates sargable, avoiding functions or type casts on indexed columns | Check for join fan-out from duplicate keys and data skew, and keep statistics up to date

text: Explain how you would sessionize raw clickstream events in SQL, where a new session starts after 30 minutes of inactivity.
ideal_key_points: Use LAG over each user's events ordered by timestamp to get the previous event time | Flag a new session when the gap exceeds 30 minutes or there is no previous event | A running SUM of the flag over the user's ordered events gives a session number | Combine user id and session number into a session id | Aggregate per session for duration, event counts and so on, and consider ties and late-arriving events

text: What is the difference between a pandas Series and a DataFrame?
ideal_key_points: A Series is a one-dimensional labeled array with a single dtype | A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labeled table of columns, where each column is a Series | Both have an index that labels rows and aligns data in operations | DataFrame columns can have different dtypes | Selecting a single column from a DataFrame returns a Series

text: What is the difference between loc and iloc in pandas?
ideal_key_points: loc selects by labels of the index and columns | iloc selects by integer position | loc slicing includes the end label while iloc slicing excludes the end position, like Python | loc supports boolean masks for filtering rows | They differ when the index is not a default zero-based range

text: Why are NumPy arrays faster than Python lists for numerical computation?
ideal_key_points: NumPy arrays store homogeneous fixed-type data in a contiguous memory block | Python lists store pointers to separate boxed Python objects | NumPy operations run in compiled C loops, avoiding Python interpreter overhead per element | Vectorized operations can use SIMD and cache-friendly access | Arrays use much less memory than lists of Python numbers

text: How would you check for and summarize missing values in a pandas DataFrame?
ideal_key_points: Use isna or isnull to get a boolean mask of missing values | Summing the mask per column gives counts and taking the mean gives the fraction missing | The info method shows non-null counts and dtypes | NaN, None and NaT represent missing values, but placeholder values like empty strings or minus 1 must be checked separately | Look at patterns such as whether missingness correlates with other columns

text: Explain how groupby works in pandas, and the difference between agg, transform and filter.
ideal_key_points: Groupby follows split-apply-combine: split rows by keys, apply a function per group, combine results | agg reduces each group to one row per group, such as sum or mean | transform returns a result the same length as the original, aligned to each row, such as a group mean per row | filter keeps or drops whole groups based on a condition | Group keys become the index unless as_index is False or reset_index is used

text: Explain the different merge types in pandas and how merge differs from concat.
ideal_key_points: merge joins DataFrames on key columns or index with how equal to inner, left, right, outer or cross | Inner keeps matching keys only, left keeps all left rows, outer keeps all rows from both | concat stacks DataFrames along rows or columns, aligning on the index rather than matching key values | Duplicate keys in a merge multiply rows | The indicator option shows where each row came from and validate checks the expected relationship

text: What strategies would you use to handle missing data, and how do you decide between them?
ideal_key_points: First understand why data is missing: completely at random, at random, or not at random | Drop rows or columns when missingness is small or a column is mostly empty | Impute with mean, median or mode, forward fill for time series, or model-based methods like KNN or iterative imputation | Add a missingness indicator feature since missingness itself can be informative | Fit imputers on training data only to avoid data leakage

text: Why is vectorization preferred over apply or Python loops in pandas? Give an example.
ideal_key_points: Vectorized operations run on whole arrays in optimized C code | apply with a Python function on rows calls the interpreter per row and is often 10 to 100 times slower | Example: multiply two columns directly instead of applying a lambda row by row | Use NumPy where or select for conditional logic and str or dt accessors for strings and dates | apply is acceptable for complex logic on small data or when no vectorized equivalent exists

text: Explain NumPy broadcasting with an example, such as subtracting each column's mean from a matrix.
ideal_key_points: Broadcasting lets arrays of different shapes combine in element-wise operations without explicit copies | Shapes are compared from the trailing dimension backward, and each dimension must be equal or 1 | A 1000 by 3 matrix minus a length-3 vector of column means works because the vector is stretched across rows | Subtracting row means needs a shape of 1000 by 1, created with reshape or keepdims | Incompatible shapes raise an error, and broadcasting avoids memory overhead of tiling

text: You need to process a 20 gigabyte CSV on a laptop with 8 gigabytes of RAM. How would you approach it?
ideal_key_points: Read in chunks using the chunksize parameter and aggregate or filter each chunk incrementally | Load only needed columns with usecols | Specify smaller dtypes such as int32, float32 and category to cut memory | Convert to a columnar format like Parquet for faster, selective reads | Use out-of-core tools such as Polars lazy mode, Dask or DuckDB that query the file without loading it all

text: What is the difference between a view and a copy in NumPy and pandas, and what does the SettingWithCopyWarning mean?
ideal_key_points: A view shares memory with the original so modifying it changes the original, while a copy is independent | Basic slicing in NumPy returns a view, while fancy or boolean indexing returns a copy | SettingWithCopyWarning appears with chained indexing where pandas cannot tell if the assignment affects the original | Fix by using a single loc call for selection and assignment, or call copy explicitly | Pandas copy-on-write mode makes derived objects behave like copies, removing this ambiguity

text: How would you reshape data between long and wide formats in pandas?
ideal_key_points: melt converts wide to long by turning columns into variable and value rows | pivot converts long to wide but fails when index and column pairs are duplicated | pivot_table handles duplicates by aggregating with a function like mean or sum | stack and unstack move levels between the row and column MultiIndex | Long format suits groupby and plotting libraries while wide suits modeling and reports

text: How would you work with time series data in pandas, for example resampling daily data to weekly and computing rolling statistics?
ideal_key_points: Convert the column with to_datetime and set it as a DatetimeIndex | resample with a weekly frequency followed by an aggregation like sum changes granularity | rolling with a window computes moving averages or sums, and windows can be time-based like 7 days | shift creates lag features and diff computes changes | Handle missing dates, time zones and avoid leakage by using only past data in features

text: After merging two DataFrames, your row count jumped from 1 million to 3 million. What happened and how would you debug it?
ideal_key_points: The join key is not unique in one or both tables, causing a one-to-many or many-to-many explosion | Check uniqueness with duplicated or value_counts on the keys in each table | Use the validate argument such as one_to_one or many_to_one to make merge fail on violations | Deduplicate or aggregate the right table before merging | Also check NaN keys, since pandas matches NaN to NaN unlike SQL, and inconsistent key formats

text: How does the category dtype save memory and speed in pandas, and when can it backfire?
ideal_key_points: Stores integer codes for each row plus a single lookup of unique categories | Large memory savings and faster groupby and comparisons for low-cardinality string columns | For high-cardinality columns with mostly unique values there is little or no benefit | Groupby on categoricals can produce rows for unobserved categories unless observed is set to True | Concatenating frames with different category sets may silently fall back to object dtype

text: Explain how NumPy arrays are laid out in memory, including strides and C versus Fortran order, and why this affects performance.
ideal_key_points: An array is a contiguous buffer plus metadata: dtype, shape and strides | Strides give the number of bytes to step in each dimension | C order is row-major, last index varies fastest, while Fortran order is column-major | Transpose and many slices are views that only change strides, producing non-contiguous arrays | Iterating along the contiguous axis is cache-friendly and faster, and some operations copy non-contiguous arrays, fixable with ascontiguousarray

text: Compare arrays and linked lists in terms of access time, insertion and deletion, and memory usage.
ideal_key_points: Arrays give O(1) random access by index because elements are contiguous | Linked lists need O(n) traversal to reach an element | Inserting or deleting in the middle of an array is O(n) due to shifting, while a linked list is O(1) once you have the node | Arrays are cache-friendly, linked lists have pointer overhead and poor locality | Dynamic arrays amortize appends to O(1)

text: What is the difference between a stack and a queue? Give a real-world use case for each.
ideal_key_points: Stack is last in first out with push and pop at the same end | Queue is first in first out, adding at the back and removing from the front | Both support core operations in O(1) | Stack uses: function call stack, undo, bracket matching, DFS | Queue uses: task scheduling, request buffering, BFS

text: What is a hash map, and what are the time complexities of lookup, insert and delete?
ideal_key_points: Stores key-value pairs, using a hash function to map keys to bucket indices in an array | Average lookup, insert and delete are O(1) | Worst case is O(n) when many keys collide | Keys must be hashable and immutable, such as strings or tuples in Python | Python dict and set are hash tables

text: How are collisions handled in a hash table?
ideal_key_points: A collision is when two keys hash to the same bucket | Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a list or tree per bucket | Open addressing probes for another empty slot using linear probing, quadratic probing or double hashing | Load factor is entries divided by buckets, and the table resizes and rehashes when it exceeds a threshold | A good hash function spreads keys uniformly, and resizing keeps average operations O(1) amortized

text: What is a binary search tree, and why can its performance degrade?
ideal_key_points: Each node's left subtree has smaller keys and the right subtree larger keys | Search, insert and delete take O(h) where h is the tree height | Balanced trees have height O(log n) | Inserting sorted data creates a skewed tree that degrades to a linked list with O(n) operations | Self-balancing trees like AVL or red-black trees guarantee O(log n)

text: What is a heap, and what operations does it support efficiently?
ideal_key_points: A complete binary tree satisfying the heap property, parent smaller than children in a min-heap | Usually stored in an array, with children of index i at 2i plus 1 and 2i plus 2 | Peek at min or max is O(1), push and pop are O(log n) | Building a heap from n elements with heapify is O(n) | Used for priority queues, top-k problems, scheduling and Dijkstra's algorithm

text: How does a dynamic array like a Python list grow, and what does amortized constant-time append mean?
ideal_key_points: Backed by a fixed-capacity array with extra reserved space | When full it allocates a larger array, typically growing by a constant factor, and copies elements | A single resize costs O(n) but happens rarely | Total cost of n appends is O(n), so the amortized cost per append is O(1) | Inserting or popping at the front is still O(n) because elements shift

text: Explain the ways to traverse a binary tree: inorder, preorder, postorder and level order.
ideal_key_points: Inorder visits left, node, right, and yields sorted order for a BST | Preorder visits node, left, right, useful for copying or serializing a tree | Postorder visits left, right, node, useful for deleting trees or computing subtree values | Level order is breadth-first using a queue | All are O(n) time, with O(h) stack space for recursive traversals and O(width) for level order

text: What is a trie, and when would you use it instead of a hash map?
ideal_key_points: A tree where each node represents a character and paths from the root spell prefixes | Insert and search take O(L) where L is the word length, independent of number of words | Efficient prefix queries like autocomplete and finding all words with a prefix, which hash maps cannot do well | Nodes store an end-of-word flag and child pointers | Memory heavy, reduced by compressed tries or radix trees

text: Compare the adjacency matrix and adjacency list representations of a graph.
ideal_key_points: Adjacency matrix uses O(V squared) space with O(1) edge existence checks | Adjacency list uses O(V plus E) space, storing neighbors per vertex | Iterating neighbors is O(degree) with a list but O(V) with a matrix | Lists suit sparse graphs, which most real graphs are, while matrices suit dense graphs | BFS and DFS run in O(V plus E) with lists and O(V squared) with a matrix

text: How would you find the k largest elements in a stream of a billion numbers?
ideal_key_points: Maintain a min-heap of size k | For each new number, if larger than the heap minimum, pop the minimum and push the new number | Time O(n log k) and space O(k), which works for streams that do not fit in memory | Sorting would be O(n log n) and need all data in memory | If data fits in memory, quickselect gives O(n) average, and in distributed settings compute top k per partition and merge

text: How would you implement a queue using two stacks, and what is the cost of each operation?
ideal_key_points: Use an inbox stack for enqueue and an outbox stack for dequeue | Enqueue pushes onto the inbox in O(1) | Dequeue pops from the outbox, and if empty first moves all inbox elements to the outbox, reversing their order | Each element is moved at most once, so dequeue is amortized O(1) | Worst case for a single dequeue is O(n)

text: Design an LRU cache that supports get and put in constant time. Explain the data structures you would use.
ideal_key_points: Combine a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency | Get looks up the node in O(1) and moves it to the front as most recently used | Put inserts or updates the node at the front, and if over capacity evicts the tail, the least recently used | Doubly linked list allows O(1) removal of an arbitrary node, and the map entry is deleted on eviction | In Python an OrderedDict with move_to_end and popitem provides the same behavior, and thread safety needs locking

text: What is a union-find or disjoint set data structure, and where is it useful?
ideal_key_points: Tracks elements partitioned into disjoint sets with find and union operations | Each set is a tree with a representative root, stored in a parent array | Path compression and union by rank or size make operations nearly O(1) amortized, the inverse Ackermann function | Used in Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, connected components and cycle detection in undirected graphs | Also used for grouping duplicates or entity resolution where links are transitive

text: How would you design a data structure that supports insert, delete and get-random-element all in average constant time?
ideal_key_points: Use a dynamic array to store values and a hash map from value to its index in the array | Insert appends to the array and records the index in the map, O(1) | Delete swaps the element with the last array element, updates the moved element's index, then pops the last element | Get random picks a uniform random index of the array in O(1) | Neither structure alone works: a hash map cannot sample uniformly and an array cannot delete arbitrary items in O(1)

text: How would you efficiently track the running median of a stream of numbers?
ideal_key_points: Use two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half | Insert each number into the appropriate heap based on comparison with the max-heap top | Rebalance so heap sizes differ by at most one | Median is the top of the larger heap, or the average of both tops when sizes are equal | Insert is O(log n) and median query is O(1), versus O(n) per insert for a sorted list

text: What does Big-O notation describe? Explain O of 1, O of log n, O of n and O of n squared with examples.
ideal_key_points: Big-O describes an upper bound on how time or space grows with input size, ignoring constants and lower-order terms | O(1) is constant time, such as array index access or hash map lookup | O(log n) halves the problem each step, such as binary search | O(n) is a single pass, such as a linear scan, and O(n squared) is nested loops, such as comparing all pairs | Worst, average and amortized cases can differ

text: Explain how binary search works and what its time and space complexity are.
ideal_key_points: Requires a sorted array or a monotonic condition | Compare the target to the middle element and discard the half that cannot contain it | Time complexity O(log n) | Space O(1) when iterative, O(log n) recursive | Careful with boundaries and off-by-one errors in loop conditions and mid updates

text: What is the difference between recursion and iteration, and what is a risk with deep recursion?
ideal_key_points: Recursion solves a problem by calling the function on smaller subproblems with a base case | Iteration uses loops and explicit state | Each recursive call uses stack space, so deep recursion can cause stack overflow | Python's default recursion limit is about 1000 | Any recursion can be converted to iteration with an explicit stack, and memoization avoids repeated work

text: Compare breadth-first search and depth-first search. When would you use each?
ideal_key_points: BFS explores level by level using a queue, DFS goes deep first using a stack or recursion | Both run in O(V plus E) time | BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs | DFS suits cycle detection, topological sort, connected components and backtracking | BFS memory grows with graph width, DFS with depth, and both need a visited set on graphs

text: Explain the two-pointer technique using the problem of finding a pair of numbers in a sorted array that sums to a target.
ideal_key_points: Place one pointer at the start and one at the end of the sorted array | If the sum is too small move the left pointer right, if too large move the right pointer left | Stop when the sum equals the target or the pointers meet | Time O(n) and space O(1), versus O(n squared) brute force | For unsorted arrays, use a hash set in O(n) time and O(n) space, or sort first in O(n log n)

text: Compare quicksort, merge sort and heap sort in terms of time complexity, space usage and stability.
ideal_key_points: Quicksort averages O(n log n) but worst case O(n squared) with bad pivots, in-place with O(log n) stack, not stable | Merge sort is always O(n log n), needs O(n) extra space, and is stable | Heap sort is O(n log n) worst case, in-place, not stable, and cache-unfriendly | Quicksort is often fastest in practice due to cache locality and randomized pivots | Python uses Timsort, a stable hybrid of merge and insertion sort that is fast on partially sorted data

text: Explain the sliding window technique using the problem of finding the longest substring without repeating characters.
ideal_key_points: Maintain a window with left and right pointers over the string | Expand the right pointer one character at a time | When a repeat appears, move the left pointer past the previous occurrence, tracked in a hash map of last seen index | Update the maximum window length at each step | Time O(n) since each pointer moves forward only, space O(size of character set)

text: Walk me through the coin change problem of finding the minimum number of coins to make an amount. Why does a greedy approach fail and how does dynamic programming solve it?
ideal_key_points: Greedy picking the largest coin can fail, for example coins 1, 3 and 4 for amount 6 gives 4, 1, 1 instead of 3, 3 | Define dp of a as the minimum coins to make amount a, with dp of 0 equal to 0 | dp of a equals 1 plus the minimum of dp of a minus c over coins c not exceeding a | Initialize unreachable amounts to infinity and return minus 1 if the target remains unreachable | Time O(amount times number of coins), space O(amount)

text: Explain your approach to finding the length of the longest increasing subsequence in an array.
ideal_key_points: Basic DP: dp of i is the LIS length ending at index i, equal to 1 plus the max dp of j for j before i with a smaller value | That approach is O(n squared) time and O(n) space | Optimized approach keeps a tails array where tails of k is the smallest ending value of an increasing subsequence of length k plus 1 | For each element binary search in tails and replace or append, giving O(n log n) | The tails array is not itself the subsequence, so reconstruction needs parent pointers

text: Explain how you would use binary search on the answer, for example to find the minimum ship capacity needed to deliver all packages within D days.
ideal_key_points: Feasibility is monotonic: if a capacity works, any larger capacity also works | Search range is from the maximum package weight to the total weight | For a candidate capacity, greedily simulate loading packages in order and count days needed in O(n) | If feasible move the upper bound down, else move the lower bound up | Total time O(n log of total weight)

text: What is the difference between memoization and tabulation in dynamic programming?
ideal_key_points: DP applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure | Memoization is top-down: recursion with a cache of computed results | Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table iteratively in dependency order | Memoization computes only needed states but has recursion overhead and depth limits | Tabulation avoids recursion and often allows space optimization by keeping only previous rows

text: How would you detect a cycle in a directed graph, and how does that relate to topological sorting?
ideal_key_points: DFS with three states, unvisited, in progress and done, where reaching an in-progress node indicates a back edge and a cycle | Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with in-degree zero using a queue | If Kahn's algorithm processes fewer than V nodes, the graph has a cycle | A topological order exists only for directed acyclic graphs | Both approaches run in O(V plus E), with applications like course scheduling and build dependencies

text: Explain Dijkstra's algorithm and when it fails.
ideal_key_points: Finds shortest paths from a source in a graph with non-negative edge weights | Uses a min-priority queue to repeatedly pick the unvisited node with the smallest tentative distance and relax its edges | Time O((V plus E) log V) with a binary heap | Fails with negative edge weights because a finalized node's distance could later improve | Use Bellman-Ford in O(V times E) for negative weights, which also detects negative cycles

text: Walk me through solving the edit distance between two strings using dynamic programming.
ideal_key_points: dp of i, j is the minimum edits to convert the first i characters of one string to the first j of the other | Base cases: dp of i, 0 equals i and dp of 0, j equals j | If characters match, dp of i, j equals dp of i minus 1, j minus 1 | Otherwise 1 plus the minimum of insert, delete and replace subproblems | Time O(m times n), space reducible to O(min of m and n) by keeping two rows

text: How would you find the median of two sorted arrays in logarithmic time?
ideal_key_points: Binary search on a partition point in the smaller array | Choose the partition in the second array so the left halves together contain half of all elements, rounded up | A valid partition has max of left A not exceeding min of right B and max of left B not exceeding min of right A | Median is the max of the left side for odd total length, or the average of max left and min right for even | Time O(log of min of m and n) and O(1) space, handling empty partitions with infinity sentinels
